19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3357
TUESDAY, 19 MAY 2015
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Budget 2015—Economic Programme
1. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: How will Budget 2015
progress the Government’s commitment to manage the Government’s finances, while
delivering better public services?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We will follow the same approach of
stable and predictable management of the Government’s finances, with the objective of
better public services for New Zealanders. We know that this is working because there
are today 42,000 fewer children living in benefit-dependent households than 3 years ago
and 194,000 new jobs compared with 4 years ago. Core Crown e xpenditure this year
will be around $4 billion lower than we thought it would be back in 2011. These
changes are making a real difference to people’s lives.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How will Budget 2015 help New Zealanders and their families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will have to wait until Budget day to see the
whole plan , but we  have already made some announcements that will benefit New
Zealand families. ACC levy cuts will bring about $500 million worth of savings to New
Zealanders. We have announced $98 million for more timely elective surgery and
improved orthopaedic treatment and also $32 million to strengthen compliance with
minimum employment standards. And we are putting $33 million towards more
immigration officers because New Zealand is such a success story that we are getting
more visitors, migrants, and tourists and need more capacity at the border.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What other Budget 2015 decisions have been announced?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We ar e providing the Inland Revenue Department with an
additional $29 million for greater property tax compliance. We already tax the gain that
people make when they sell a property that they bought with the intention of reselling it,
and that is fair. We are s harpening up those rules to make it easier for the Inland
Revenue Department to enforce them and help ensure that people understand their
liabilities. So everyone will have to provide their IRD number on every property they
buy, other than their main home,  and everyone will know there will be a 2 -year
brightline test, meaning that gains from property sold within 2 years of purchase will be
taxed, except if it is the main place of residence, or inherited, or part of a matrimonial
settlement.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he recall saying in the 2014 Budget speech “There will be a
small surplus next year , and increasing surpluses are forecast over time.” , and now,
having broken that promise, will he be using exactly the same sentence in this year’s
Budget speech?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do remember making that statement as part of the 2014
Budget, and it indicated significant progress from an $18 billion deficit to what will turn
out to be a $500 million or $600 million deficit. It falls short of the surplus that was
budgeted by a bit, and that means we will achieve surplus next year.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What particular measures in Bu dget 2015 apply to property investors
who may be based overseas?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As well as having to supply a New Zealand IRD number, all
non-resident—that is, non - tax resident—buyers and sellers must also provide their tax
3358 Oral Questions  19 May 2015
ID number from their home country, along with a current ID such as a passport. This
will enable the Inland Revenue Department to share tax information with overseas
authorities. Also, to ensure that our full anti  - money-laundering rules apply to non -
residents, they must have a New Zealand bank account before they get a New Zealand
IRD number. Finally, we will be looking at introducing a withholding tax for non - tax
residents, which, if adopted, means we will take the tax off immediately when the
property is sold, and the foreign owner will have to square up with the Inland Revenue
Department later.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: How does the increased compliance on property gains fit within the
Government’s response to escalating Auckland house prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The real issue in Auckland is that there are too few houses to
meet demand. So the problem is pretty simple, but ensuring more supply is the most
effective long-term tool for bringing some order to the Auckland property market. So
we are working on a number of fronts: changes in the tax regime, which may dampen
demand; setting up special housing areas to free up more land; and concentrating on
redeveloping extensive Government landholdings in Auckland —for instance,
transferring Housing New Zealand properties to the Tāmaki Redevelopment Company.

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: How do those decisions sit within the Government’s commitment to
control its spending?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: These commitments are all being financed by  a relatively
low level of new Government initiatives. So, for instance, the total annual cost of new
initiatives in this Government’s last six Budgets is around $3 billion. The last six
Budgets of the previous Government had $20 billion of new initiatives , and at the end
of that time, even supporters of it, such as the Salvation Army, were led to conclude that
despite all the spending, there were no better outcomes for New Zealand communities.
With less new spending we are getting better outcomes.
Housing Market—Auckland
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that there is no housing crisis in Auckland in light of the fact the
average Auckland house price has risen by $100,000 in the past year and the Reserve
Bank says this is “increasing the risk of financial instability”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because over the last few years I have
heard many overstated claims of a crisis in various parts of the economy. The previous
one was apparently in manufacturing. The Government and the Reserve Bank have both
acknowledged that we need more houses bui lt in Auckland and we need to make that
happen faster. That is why the Government has taken significant action to increase
supply and speed up land development.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he introduced a measure that looks like a capital gains tax,
but which he says is not one, to fight an Auckland property market that is in crisis, but
which he says is not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Just to quote Mr Little, he said the policy is “not a capital
gains tax”. What we have done is said that  for anyone who is an investor in a 2 -year
period, we will take the ambiguity out of the current situation because we believe that
that is reasonable. And for foreigners whom we do not have good records on in New
Zealand—yes, they will be forced to pay their fair share of tax.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of his finance Minister’s comment that it is “a bit unclear”
what impact his new measures will have, by how much does he say the new brightline
test will slow the growth of Auckland house prices; and if he does not know, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, we have not modelled that, but what I can say is that, of
the additional money we are putting into inspectors —which is $29 million in this
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3359
Budget and $33 million from Budget  2013, which is yet to be spent; that is $62
million—the expectation is that we will get $420 million. The reason we are likely to
get at least $420 million, if not more, is that the ambiguity is removed. I will say,
though, that the intention test has bee n around for a very long period of time. Funnily
enough, and I have not actually bothered to go and look at it, if one was to go back and
look at all the advice that the previous Labour Government got when house prices
doubled under its watch, one would pr obably look at this issue as an issue that was
raised back then. But guess what? Labour did nothing; National acts.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How many property speculators who are not already caught by the
intention test will be caught by the brightline test; and if he does not know, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The analysis of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment suggests that between 17 and 18 percent of Auckland’s housing
transactions currently involve houses being boug ht and sold within 2 years. I would be
pretty surprised if all of those owners are paying tax on that, and I would strongly
suggest that quite a few more will as a result of the brightline test.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he announced a tax pol icy when he does not know how
well it will work, whom it will catch, or what the rules even are?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I know whom it will catch, and they are people who buy and
sell an investment property within 2 years. They are foreigners w ho are currently non -
resident income taxpayers who are not paying their fair share of tax. Yes, the
Government takes a careful and cautious approach in this regard, but that is the right
thing to do because, in the end, taxpayers are entitled to have som e clarity in what they
are doing. But I do think, and the Government has thought this for quite a long period of
time, that the intention test needs reflecting upon, and that was the very reason why we
asked the Inland Revenue Department to look at this ve ry issue back in 2010. The
officials in 2010 said they did not think we should move on it; in 2015 they changed
their minds.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why will he not just be straight with New Zealanders and admit that
his new policies will not fix th e Auckland housing crisis, and that he is just doing the
bare minimum and hoping the problem will go away because he does not have a clue
what to do?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Under this Government we have special housing areas of
which there are about 90 in Auckland. Under this Government we have reduced the
duty on imported materials. Under this Government we have reformed the Resource
Management Act, and we are looking to do more. Under this Government we have
introduced a new brightline test fo r those who buy and sell investment properties. We
have done a lot in the housing area. I know that Labour members do not like it, but
house prices doubled under their watch. Actually, Auckland house prices went up by 79
percent under the previous Labour G overnment. When they asked Andrew Little last
week what—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister will resume his
seat.
Housing Market—Overseas Buyers
3. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he stand by the following statements: in May last
year, “There is no housing crisis in Auckland.”; also in May last year, “I do not believe
there is a crisis in housing.”; in June last year, “It’s not a crisis.”; in April this yea r, “So
3360 Oral Questions  19 May 2015
I don’t think you could call it a crisis.”; and just last month, “I don’t believe a capital
gains tax works.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I stand by all of those statements. Interestingly enough, if
you look at the information by the Re al Estate Institute, figures across New Zealand
actually show that although Auckland house prices are up, the rest of the country is very
mixed; some are actually down. And, interestingly enough, if you look at the equivalent
period of time under the last Labour Government, house prices doubled. Under National
they have gone up nationally by 35 percent.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he stand by this statement, made by himself: “I don’t
believe foreigners buying the odd house in New Zealand is what’s driving the escalation
of prices”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I believe that statement is correct. I think that there is
quite a degree of confusion, actually, about the people who buy houses in New Zealand,
who may come from ove rseas originally or may not be Caucasian. But I think the
number of very large purchases of properties in New Zealand that are from offshore is
likely to be quite a low number—lower than what people expect, in my view.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston  Peters
items.text: Does he agree with Lyndon Fairbairn of All Property —
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Will the Leader of the House contain himself. Will the
member please start his supplementary question again.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Pe ters
items.text: Does he agree with Lyndon Fairbairn of All Property
Solutions, who, when asked on Morning Report this morning whether the Government’s
measures will be strenuous on foreign buyers, replied “No, not at all.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That is  an interesting view that the gentleman might have —
and I do not know who he is. But let us put it this way. If the rules are, as they will be,
that a foreign buyer or a non - resident taxpayer—because that is the test, actually, a non
- resident tax status —has to provide their IRD number, has to provide a New Zealand
bank account, and, by the way, by the middle of next year will have withholding tax
taken off any sales of properties, and they will then have to reverse the burden to get
that tax back. If that is no effect, then that is a very interesting world that that gentleman
lives in, but I would suggest it is one that is quite a long way away from reality.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why does he not just stop tinkering around the edges  and,
to use his words, “get some guts” and back New Zealand buyers, and stop foreign non -
residents buying New Zealand land and houses?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We know Mr Peters’ views about foreign investment and the
likes into New Zealand. But , interestingly enough, maybe the member, when he returns
back to his office for a nice cup of tea this afternoon, might want to have a look on the
Sydney Morning Herald website, where they actually talk quite openly about how house
prices are rising much faster there than they are in Auckland. And the article goes on to
say: “It would be nice if there was a single guilty party —foreigners, investors, negative
gearing, local Government, capital gains discounts, cheap money, population growth —
but it’s much more complicated” than all of those.
Child Support—Reforms
4. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “we believe the strong underlying
economy and responsible fiscal management can deliver a surplus when the final
Government accounts are published next October”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I stand by my full statement made at
the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, which was: “falling dairy prices and low
inflation are restricting growth in the nominal economy and Government revenue. This
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3361
makes it more challenging for the Government to  achieve surplus in 2014-15. However,
we remain on track to reduce debt to 20 per cent … by 2020. Although this latest
Treasury forecast predicts a small deficit for the current year, we believe the strong
underlying economy … can deliver a surplus when th e final Government accounts are
published next October,”.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he explain to the House how it is an example of “responsible
fiscal management” to allow a blowout in expenditure from $34 million to $210 million
for the upgrade of the Child Support system at the Inland Revenue Department?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member may want to delve into the details of that. As I
recall it, at least a fair bit of the expenditure came from two sources. One was that the
complexity of the proposals was underestimated while trying to take into account the
income of multiple parents with regard to particular children. Further changes were then
made by the select committee, which made it even more expensive. Underlying the
expense is the fact that the Inland Revenue Department’s computer system is now so
old that it costs an enormous amount of money to make relatively small changes. That is
why we are investing in a 5 to 10 -year programme to upgrade the Inland Revenue
Department’s system. We believe that children deserving the support of their separated
parents cannot wait aroun d until the Inland Revenue Department’s system is all
changed.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How is it “responsible fiscal management” to ignore the advice of
Treasury, which told him “We believe the costs of the proposed change outweigh the
benefits.” and which recommended postponing or not proceeding with the proposal?
How is that responsible?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member may be surprised, but the Government quite
often disagrees with Treasury. Occasionally I wish it would agree wit h Treasury more,
but it quite often disagrees with it. In this case, the Government decided that it needed
to make changes to what was a 25 -year-old formula for child support. Families
constitute themselves differently these days and there are different se ts of expectations,
so we went ahead.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek the leave of the House to table a memo from Treasury,
dated 6 August 2012, in which it recommends postponing or not proceeding—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been described. I will put the leave.
Leave is sought to table this particular memo from Treasury. Is there any objection?
There is none.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How is it “responsible fiscal management” to ignore the further
advice of Treasury, the State Services Commission, and the Government Chief
Information Officer, which recommended that the delivery of the Child Support system
reforms be discontinued despite the large sunk costs?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: They didn’t get elected.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think my colleague Minister Brownlee made exactly the
right point. In the end, the Government makes decisions, as the elected representative,
about what it believes is going to work for the community. Officials saw that the costs
were higher than expected. The Government decided to incur those costs; they did not. I
have to say that it is more fiscally responsible than that member protesting for excessive
wage increases and now saying that the Government should prop up a failing social
services provider—more money for every problem.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek the leave of the House to table an email from  Treasury,
dated Tuesday, 18 February 2014 at 2.51 p.m., with advice from Treasury, the State
3362 Oral Questions  19 May 2015
Services Commission, and the Government Chief Information Officer that the Child
Support—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been described enough fo r the House. I
will put the leave. Leave is sought to table that particular email. Is there any objection?
There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Can we ask Treasury what Labour’s policy is?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Hundreds of millions of dollars being wasted is funny, is it,
Gerry?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I have called Gran t Robertson to ask
his supplementary question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is one of the reasons that he will not be delivering a surplus in
this Budget, or any meaningful changes on child poverty, because he wasted hundreds
of millions of dollars pursuing a project that all of his key advisers on fiscal, State
sector, and technology issues told him to bin?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, and the member should try to get his head around what
changes have been made to child s upport. As he wil l know, as a constituency MP, for
the last 20 years families have been complaining about the way the formula works. It is
always difficult to change it, but it was changed in ways that Parliament and the select
committee decided were fair. It did cost more  than was expected. The Government
came to the view that it was in the interests of the tho usands of families affected by
child support to make those changes.
Accident Compensation Corporation—Levies
5. SARAH DOWIE (National —Invercargill) to the Minister for ACC : What
indicative reductions to ACC levies are signalled in Budget 2015?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Budget 2015 will s ignal that ACC is on
track to provide further levy cuts of around $375 million in 2016-17 and $120 million in
2017-18. These indicative levy cuts represent a total saving for New Zealanders of
around $500 million and will be spread across the motor vehicle , work, and earners
accounts. The indicative reductions, if confirmed, will take total levy cuts since 2012 to
around $2 billion, benefiting all New Zealanders. These cuts are possible only because
of good financial management. This is great news for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: What factors could see these indicative levy reductions change?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Although there could be some change to the total amount into
the per year amounts, the Government is committed to reducti ons of at least $500
million across the three accounts. Before the Government makes final decisions on levy
reductions this year, ACC will consult under existing legislation with levy payers and
make a recommendation. The final decision will take into acco unt other factors like
claim numbers and discount rates. It is important to understand that the exact amounts
for each year may vary depending on the consultation. However, I can confirm
reductions of at least $500 million—and that is $2 billion since 2012.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: What recent announcements has the Government made about
improving the transparency of the levy-setting process?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Last week I introduced the Accident Compensation (Financial
Responsibility and Tra nsparency) Amendment Bill to the House. The bill will make a
number of amendments to the Act to improve the levy -setting framework. The bill will
also amend the Act to allow the collection of residual levies to be discontinued earlier.
New principles will be introduced into the legislation to ensure greater levy stability and
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3363
solvency over the long term. The Government will be required to publish a funding
policy and the long -term implications of levy decisions. This will ensure there is
maximum transparency around ensuring enough money is available to pay the lifetime
cost of people’s injuries. It is also my hope that levy payers can see levies are as low as
possible while ensuring our most vulnerable have greater security for the long term.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: What reports has she seen on alternative approaches to setting ACC
levies?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I have seen a report about people suggesting going back to a
pay-as-you-go approach. The advice I have had is that this would lead to h igher costs
for claims and increasing levy rates over the long term. It would also be a big step
backwards for some of our most vulnerable New Zealanders whose quality of life
depends on long -term rehabilitation. It would also mean less certainty and stabi lity for
New Zealand businesses. These reports come from Andrew Little at the same time that
Labour has removed its ACC policy from its website. He needs to front up to New
Zealand and actually tell people whether Labour’s plan is to raid the ACC coffers.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Why will she not cut levies immediately, as recommended by the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, by Treasury, and by ACC itself; and
what possible excuse does she have for overcharging ACC levies now that the
Government will not even get to its promised surplus?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: We are cutting ACC le vies now. There is $480 million  worth
of cuts this year. There are several reasons why we have put a 2 -year, $500 million
policy in. The first reason is that there is still volatility in the accounts. The second
reason that—[Interruption] You need to listen to this, Labour members. If you go down
too far in terms of levy reductions, the overall levy path over the years means that you
can have increases in the out-years. The members are going to have to understand this.

items.speaker: The facts are
items.text: $2 billion since 2012 compared with a $480 million hole under members
on that side of the House.
Child Poverty—Measurement
6. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How poor does a child need to be under his “definitional difference”,
which he told Paul Henry about yesterday, when he claimed that there were only 60,000
to 100,000 children living in poverty?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The advice I have from the Ministry of Social Development
material deprivation index is that there are indeed between 60,000 and 100,000 children
who are living in more severe material hardship. They are children who, based on that
index, lack nine to 11 items from that deprivation index.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Under his “definitional difference”, is a child living in poverty if
their parents cannot afford to buy them fresh food, if they do not have two pairs of
shoes, if they cannot afford a school uniform, and if they do not have their own bed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I refer the member to the Ministry of Social Development’s
material deprivation index.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Children’s Commissioner wrong, and are his experts who
worked on the s olutions to child poverty wrong when they state that there are between
180,000 and 200,000 children who are materially deprived —that is, they go without
three or more essential items such as fresh food, warm clothes, their own bed, and good
shoes?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It seems to me that the member picks and chooses her index
depending on what suits her argument, but all I can tell the member is that if one looks
3364 Oral Questions  19 May 2015
at the number of children who are deemed to be at the most significant level of
deprivation in New Zealand based on the Ministry of Social Development index, it is
60,000 to 100,000. But I would say that this Government is very focused on all children,
particularly those who are less well off, and there are degrees of how less well off they
are. That is why the Government introduced free GP visits. That is why the Government
has put more money into providers like KidsCan. That is why this Government has
worked alongside Fonterra and Sanitarium to provide free breakfasts. That is why the
Government has supported having social workers in all low-decile schools. It is why the
Government has introduced Children’s T eams to work with at -risk children and
families. That is why the Government has insulated every State house, and it is why the
Government has  worked to insulate 240,000 other homes and has given them clean
heating. This is a Government that, in the very worst of times in New Zealand, has
maintained benefits and entitlements that provide support for the very children whom
that member is talking about.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Did the Ministry of Social Development fail to give him the 2014
Bryan Perry report that showed that there are 260,000 children in poverty and that
205,000 of them are living in severe poverty, where their parents earn  less than half the
median income?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member will note —if she wants to refer to that particular
report that she is talking about —how consistently the numbers that she is talking about
have been at that level of deprivati on. In fact, there were about 240,000 to 260,000
children living in poverty under Labour, at the height of what was theoretically an
economic boom. But what I can say is that Bryan Perry’s new annual report —and the
new edition will be out very soon —will make it quite clear that in terms of what they
define as severe material hardship, there are between 60,000 and 100,000 children, and
they have between nine and 11 conditions on the deprivation index.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Would the Prime Minister a gree that by promising to tackle child
poverty and then changing the definition of poverty to exclude most of the children who
are actually poor, he is breaking yet another Budget promise?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member is being extr emely selective with the
comments I have made. If she actually goes back and looks at the interviews that I have
done on this topic ever since the last election, she will see that I have consistently said
that there is a disagreement between ourselves and those who claim that there are
260,000 children in that category. We have made it quite clear that we see a group of
60,000 to 100,000 as our priority. It does not mean that we do not provide either
services or support for the wider group; we actually do. I listed a great many, and I will
not repeat them now. But our primary area of focus and attention is on those who are
most in need. I think most New Zealanders, actually, would say that the Government
having a focus on those who are in the worst of condit ions is putting our resources in
the right place.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does he stand by his previous statements in this House that there
are many measures of child poverty, in light of his position now that there is just one,
material deprivation, which just so happens to be the smallest of all the measures that
are used by the Children’s Commissioner?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I stand by the view that there is no one single measure, but I
am simply saying that the material deprivation index, according to the advice that we
have had from the Ministry of Social Development, is the best. That is one measure, but
there is no one single measure of poverty in New Zealand, and I do not think there
should be.
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3365

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will  the Prime Minister just admit that he has made up an Oliver
Twist definition of poverty so that he can ignore some 200,000 New Zealand children
who suffer from poverty every day?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member risks being a little b it silly. I listed a few
moments ago a very wide range of support that we provide for all New Zealand
children, and in some cases, obviously, the support is much more focused on those who
are in need. I have made it quite clear that I think there is a grou p who are in worse
hardship than others, and that is supported by the material deprivation index, which
evolved, actually, from the European equivalent. It is a very thoughtful process that
Bryan Perry goes through, and it looks at very detailed analysis. I am more than happy
to have the debate with the New Zealand public, but I think you might find that the New
Zealand public supports the view that those who are most in need deserve the most
support. That does not mean that other children do not get support; they actually do. But
this Government is very focused on that group, and I think most New Zealanders would
say that is the right thing to do. The member shakes her head, but if we followed her
economic policies a whole million of New Zealand children wo uld be in hardship
because none of their parents would be in work.

Information and Communications Technology Industry—Performance
8. JONO NAYLOR (National) to the Minister for Economic Development: What
progress is the Government making in developing New Zealand’s ICT sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Last week I, along
with the Hon Amy Adams, released the New Zealand 2015 Information and
Communications Technology Report . This report provides in -depth analysis of New
Zealand’s information an d communications technology sector and showcases New
Zealand’s very strong performance over the last few years in this sector, with the
positive support of the Government. The report shows that the sector has been growing
at the rate of 9 percent per year since 2008. The industry is expanding. The number of
IT businesses has topped 10,000 for the first time and IT stocks now make up about 10
percent of the value of all listings on the New Zealand Exchange main board, compared
with 1 percent 5 years ago. It is clear that New Zealand’s information and
communications technology sector is an increasingly important contributor to our
economy, both as a strong platform for future business growth and as the driver of the
digitisation of our economy.

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: How is New Zealand’s information and communications technology
industry performing on the world stage?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Very well. Exports have grown at 14 percent a year in the
information and communications technology sec tor—that is, 14 percent a year —over
the last 6 years, and are now worth just shy of $1 billion a year at $930 million; a
doubling in value since 2008. To succeed internationally it is important our companies
are linked with the world and encouraged to develop their products and ideas when they
enter new markets. We are doing that through the roll -out of ultra -fast broadband,
through partnering with Callaghan Innovation to encourage research and development,
and by working with New Zealand Trade and Enterpri se to make the most of
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3367
opportunities offshore. The information and communications technology industry is just
one example of a number of industries that are expanding and diversifying New
Zealand’s economic base with the encouragement of this Government.
Greenhouse Gas Emissions—Treasury Forecasts
9. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister for Climate

items.speaker: Change Issues
items.text: What is the range of potential costs to the Government resulting from
New Zealand’s current forecast for increasing net greenhouse gas emissions for the
period 2021-2030, as reported in the Treasury’s climate change briefing dated 6 October

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The range of figures
contained in the redacted part of that now rather dated document was between 0.3 and
0.8 percent of GDP and, crucially, even at the very highest levels of carbon prices used,
took no impact whatsoever on our emissions. Happily, I can inform the member that a
lot more professional work has gone into modelling since then. Only yesterday we
published modelling that has involved a range of agencies, including the New Zealand
Treasury, which puts the cost of a minus 0.5 percent target between 2020 and 2030 at
the rather more reasonable cost of $3.6 billion —not a small sum of money but not
nearly large enough to meet the member’s political narrative.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of that answer, what exactly did Treasury get wrong
when it said in this paper that the cost to the Government of not cutting our greenhouse
gas emissions was up to $52 billion—as Treasury said in this paper?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I think what Treasury got wrong was that it did not use
sufficiently sophisticated software to conceal the redacted information.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: It is nice of you to admit  that, Minister. Why is it that the
Government’s climate target consultation paper makes the unsubstantiated claim that
the annual cost of cutting emissions is up to $1,800 per household but does not happen
to mention Treasury’s rather detailed analysis th at says that the cost of not cutting
emissions is up to $3,400 per household—if we do not cut emissions?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Well, we will let modellers debate the relative merits of these
models. What we have done is commission a first-class piece by Infometrics with all the
agents involved, and the figure they have come up with is the figure the member
mentioned.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So is the Minister finally admitting that the redacted number in
this paper for the cost to the Government of not cutting emissions is up to $52 billion?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: No, I am not verifying that. That was a matter of a so -called
independent forecaster drawing two dots together that really should never have been
joined together. I recommend to the member and the members of this House that they
look at the very professional analysis that we put on the Ministry for the Environment’s
website only yesterday.
Buildings, Earthquake-prone—Strengthening Requirements
10. BRETT HUDSON (National) to the Minister for Building and Housing: What
changes is the Government proposing to ensure New Zealand is more resilient to the
significant risks we face from earthquakes?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: We have made two
significant announcements. The first is about taking a more targeted approach to
strengthening older buildings. We have zoned New Zealand into three categories of risk
and have varied time frames to upgrade  accordingly. We have also sped up the time
frame for strengthening higher risk buildings like schools, hospitals, and other
emergency buildings in medium and high risk areas. The result of these changes will
3368 Oral Questions  19 May 2015
reduce the estimated cost, in net present value terms, by about $500 million, while at the
same time retain the safety gains of 330 fewer deaths and 360 fewer serious injuries.
Today I have also made an nouncements about post -emergency building management.
We are ensuring that we learn the lessons from the experience after the Christchurch
earthquakes, so that we manage our building stock as efficiently as possible so that
people can get into their buildi ngs quickly, and also so that we ensure public safety.
This is part of the Government’s broader programme for ensuring we are more resilient
to these risks.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: What response has he had to taking a more risk -focused approach to
the strengthening requirements for older buildings?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Government’s revised approach to earthquake
strengthening has been widely welcomed. The Institution of Professional Engineers
New Zealand Inc., Local Government New  Zealand, and the Property Council New
Zealand have all endorsed the approach. Fundamental to it is understanding that the
level of risk from earthquakes varies very significantly around New Zealand, as
reinforced by the report today from GNS Science. In this city, an MM8 earthquake has
got a frequency of once every 120 years, and in Auckland, of only once in every 7,400
years, so it is appropriate that our response takes into account that sort of risk profile.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: How do the change s on post -disaster building management
announced today learn from the tragic experience of the Christchurch earthquakes?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think every member of this House can recall the huge
tension about post -earthquake management after the earthquakes in 2010 and 2011.
Some owners and tenants of buildings were incredibly frustrated that they were not able
to get access, and t here was confusio n about the stickering system. S o, consistent with
the recommendations of the royal commission of inquiry, we have changed that system.
We are proposing to make changes to the Building Act, and I am confident that with
these changes, were New Zealand —hopefully not—to experience a similar earthquake,
we would be far better prepared to be able to manage those safety risks and, at the same
time, get people access to their buildings more quickly.

Zealanders benefit from the growing economy with a focus on children who are living
in hardship”?

items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: How many children living in poverty have benefited from the
growing economy while her Government has been in office?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: As we have heard before, there are a number of ways of
measuring poverty. What we do know is that in the long term children who live in
homes that are dependent on a benefit have considerably worse outcomes in life than
those who do not. This Government has seen the number of children living in benefit -
dependent households fall by almost 42,000 over the last 3 years.

19 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3371
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 7 May.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I am pleased to stand again to take my 4 minutes on
the Environmental Reporting Bill. This is an excellent bill. I just want to recap a little
bit about the actual bill itself, given that it has been a whole week since we have been
away on an adjournment break. I just want to bring it all back and give a bit of an
overview on the bill itself.
This bill creates a national level environmental reporting syst em. It ensures that
reporting on our environment occurs on a regular basis and that it can be trusted —
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise for interrupting the member. There is too much
noise both in the Chamber from members leaving a nd also from the gallery. If people
wish to leave, I would be grateful if they did so more quietly.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: As I was saying, the report can be trusted by the public because
it is conducted by an independent, fair, and accurate person. I will talk a little bit more
about that particular person.
The provisions of the bill require reports from five key domains, and they are
atmosphere, climate, air, freshwater, and marine domains. These are set out, as I said,
by independent reviewers, and  they are the Secretary for the Environment and the
Government Statistician. They will also be responsible for making sure that there is a
synthesis report that will look across domains at trends and interactions, once every 3
years. It also ensures that t he producers of our reports are independent. That is what I
was saying about the Government Statistician and the Secretary for the Environment. It
also allows our Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, who holds a very
important independent role, to be able to give some strong analysis and review on the
reports being produced.
When I last stood here I talked about the marine environment, and I talked a little bit
about the exclusive economic zone legislation that we are putting in. This is making
sure that we take out the potential risks and activities within the marine environment,
like petroleum exploration, seabed mining, marine energy generation, and carbon
capture development, while making the Environmental Protection Authority responsible
for consenting and enforcing these activities, which is all part and parcel of the water
domain, which I spoke about quite in depth the last time I spoke in this debate.
Finally, I just want to talk about the air domain. This is really important. Just recently
I was in Christchurch at an event hosted by the Electricity Networks Association. They
talked about the various things that they are doing within the provision of cars run by
electricity. This is actually helping to reduce emissions into the environment. They also
showed us where they proposed to put, I suppose, all their plug -in areas —instead of
petrol stations—that electric cars can park up in to be recharged so they can make the
journey. That is from the top of the North Island all the way to the bottom  of the South
Island.
I believe that this is a very good bill. It is a strong bill. It is the first time that we have
had a bill that looks at our environment. It has a step change that we implemented in
2011, and I commend the bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. James
Shaw—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: I rise to speak on the Environmental Reporting Bill. The
Green Party would have liked to be able to support this bill because we do suffer in this
3372 Environmental Reporting Bill 19 May 2015
country from a lack of information about the state of our environment. We did support
the referral of the En vironmental Reporting Bill to the Local Government and
Environment Committee. Unfortunately, we are not able to support the bill in its later
stages because of the lack of independence over who is going to be determining what
gets reported on.
I started my career at PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK, where we were starting to
look at non -financial indicators of reporting, and that included environmental capital,
natural capital, social capital, intellectual capital, and so on. What was critically
important was that the public and investors actually understood that the criteria that
were being reported against were independent and not determined by the company that
was being reported on. This bill kind of fails that standard.
One of the previous speakers on this bill did say that they felt that it is better to be
doing something than nothing, and given that we have such woeful inadequacy around
our reporting at the moment, that is not an unreasonable argument to make, except that
doing something like this and  enabling Ministers to be able to determine what gets
reported on is actually worse than doing something. It is a bit like the Government’s
approach to climate change. You see, having an emissions trading scheme enables the

items.speaker: Government to say
items.text: “We’re doing our bit. We’ve got an emissions trading scheme.” But
given that actual emissions are increasing, and will increase by net 48 percent by 2020,
it is actually saying: “Well, it’s OK. We’re doing our bit. We’ve got in place an
emissions trading scheme. We’re one of the world leaders.” But if your actual emissions
are increasing, then the policy has no impact and you might as well not do it. It is
merely a smokescreen.
Unfortunately, because of clause 18 in this bill, we cannot support it through to the
later stages. There are a number of options to solve this. One is that the Government
Statistician could simply decide what the areas to be reported on are going to be.
Another option is that the areas that are going to be reported on could actually be laid
down in law. I have a member’s bill in the ballot at the moment called the Public
Finance (Sustainable Development Indicators) Amendment Bill, which actually covers
a number of different areas that would be laid down in legislation, if we were interested
in ac tually having an independent set of criteria where we said: “Well, these are the
things that we ought to be reporting on.”
We can only have credible reporting of any kind, including environmental reporting,
if it is independent and free from the interfere nce of Ministers. Unfortunately, this bill
does not do that. The Minister here actually does have full control over what gets
reported. I think that the chair of the Local Government and Environment Committee,
during his speech on the bill earlier, said th at this is exactly the same as in our financial
reporting. It actually is not. What gets reported in our financial reporting is actually laid
down in law.
I am sorry to say that we are unable to support this bill. We did support it through to
select commi ttee. We note that there were well over 300 submitters, and the vast
majority of them talked about this matter of independence. I think that if this was an
education report, we would have to finish with the words “must try harder”. With that, I
am afraid that the Green Party will not be supporting this bill through to its next stage.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: I am pleased to join in opposition
to this bill, for the reasons  that have been outlined by Mr Shaw. Although the Labour
Party supports the intent of this bill —and we did support it at the first reading —
unfortunately, the main thrust of the bill is its lack of independence. It is all great to
have experienced officials —the Government Statistician and the Secretary for the
Environment—involved in producing these reports. However, the actual topics that
those reports will cover are completely in the domain of the Government.
19 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3373

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It’s not true.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIK ATENE
items.text: It is true. Therefore, there is no better example of our
opposition to this bill than the speech from the member who just resumed her seat
earlier, Ms Hayes, because she talked about the so -called independence; she talked
about the  wonderful work that has been going on in the various domains —water
quality, air, and various other domains that are covered by this bill. However —and I am
referring back to her speech, before she was interrupted the week before last —she was
basically givi ng us the Government’s spin lines, through its blue -tinted lenses, as to
what it is doing around the environment. That is the very reason why we are opposing
this bill, because that is the very reason why it lacks independence.
We are the only country in the OECD that does not have a legislative basis for
independent environmental reporting. All Kiwis want to know and be sure that we have
trusted, independent reports on the state of our environment. That is critical. This bill
fails. It completely fails, b ecause the actual content, the topics that will be covered by
these periodic reports—be they on the domains or the other sequential -type reports that
will be coming—will be completely set in place by regulation through the Ministers. So
it lacks independence.
But I also want to touch on the irony of the Government because just prior to the last
time we were debating this bill we were debating a bill on the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund. The members opposite were lauding the virtues of the
independence of  the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. I believe it was Mr Bishop
who said in his speech that we are politicians and we are not best placed to make
investment decisions. Well, the same could be applied to this independent
environmental reporting. We are pol iticians—that is right —and we are not best placed
to make decisions or to actually provide independent reports on the state of our
environment. It was demonstrated by Ms Hayes and Mr Bishop that this Government is
lost. It really has not got a clue in term s of what is required for providing independent
reporting on the state of our environment.
It is a shame on this Government that it is pushing this bill through when there are
deep flaws in it—deep flaws. We need to make sure —and this is very important; i t is a
very important topic—that we have independent reporting on our environment. Well, let
us make it independent. Let us take the topics out of the realm of the Ministers, and let
us make sure that the independent Government officials who are charged by  statute—
that is the irony again. If we look at clause 14, I believe it is, the statute says that the
Government officials —the Government Statistician and the Secretary for the
Environment—have to act independently of the Government. That in itself shows y ou
how flawed the bill is, because how can you have an independent report when the actual
topics that will be considered in the report are actually cooked up by the Ministers
themselves?
Sure, the Ministers may have to consult and follow a statutory proces s around how
they finalise the decisions, but at the end of the day the decisions, the topics that will be
covered under the reports, are completely the domain of the Ministers. Therefore the
reports lose all credibility—all credibility—and that is why we oppose this bill. Cheers.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It is an honour to rise to support this
very important bill, the Environmental Reporting Bill, on its second reading. Can I firs t
acknowledge the work of our environment Minister, the Hon Dr Nick Smith, for his
work in the space of protecting our environment in New Zealand. Also, I acknowledge
our Local Government and Environment Committee chair, Scott Simpson, for the
dispensing o f a very busy select committee, and also the previous select committee
chair, the Hon Maggie Barry.
3374 Environmental Reporting Bill 19 May 2015
I was not on the select committee at the time of the submissions but, reading them
through, overall it is time for this environmental reporting system to b e implemented.
This bill creates a national-level environmental reporting system to ensure that reporting
on our environment occurs on a regular basis. This is important, so it can be trusted —so
the public can trust it as independent, fair, and accurate in formation. Why is that
important? Because there are people, parties, and organisations that through political or
financial motives want to bring down our clean and green image of New Zealand.
A good example of this was a few years ago when the British Gre en Party decided it
would come up with an approach that our lamb production —growing our lamb in New
Zealand and exporting it overseas to the UK—had a bigger carbon footprint than locally
produced lamb. As you would expect in the consumer-driven market in the UK, it led to
a drop in New Zealand lamb sales in the UK and drove up locally produced lamb
production in the UK, until some bright sparks at Lincoln University got together and
used evidence—they used research and science —and reported that, in fact, ev en with
the lamb production in New Zealand and the carbon footprint of sending our lamb by
plane to the UK, we still had a smaller carbon footprint than British -produced meat.
That was because of the intensification of their farming. This is a good example  of why
we need this environmental reporting system in order to provide independent, fair, and
accurate information to the public, so that it will inform and enable informed discussion
and debate.
This Government has a great record of environmental manage ment and of balancing
our environmental responsibilities, plus our economic opportunities, to preserve and
protect our natural environment. It is amazing that we are the only OECD country that
currently does not have an environmental reporting system of th is standard. So, once
again, it takes a National Government to bring in this first for this country, very much
like it has brought in the Environmental Protection Authority to protect the environment
in the petroleum exploration space, as well as our fresh water standards to ensure that
our rivers come up to a national standard and that any rivers that are below that standard
are focused on to ensure we have a national standard of freshwater quality and
management. Quite simply, you cannot manage what you do not measure.
I suppose that if I reflect on my career in health care before I got into politics, we
used the Hawthorne effect, which basically says that when you start measuring
something you focus on it and the performance will naturally increase and im prove
behind that—the Hawthorne effect. It is quite right that we cannot manage this unless
we measure it. It is right that we start measuring it through this environmental reporting
system. A key part of reporting, data analysis, and interpretation is we have to move
past the data quality debate. What happens is that every time we have a report, people
who just want to attack it, for whatever reason, will resort to asking: “Is the data quality
correct?” and “Is the data valid?”. Having this environmental r eporting framework will
ensure that.
A good example is found by going to the Salvation Army’s state of the nation report
this year. Its state of the nation report demonstrated that child poverty was tracking
downwards. It stated that it had handed out few er food parcels than previous years. Was
the first question that was asked: how do we support that continual decline in poverty
and food parcels being handed out? No; it was: how can you ensure there is correct data
quality? It is right that because we wil l have this environmental reporting framework,
we will move the discussion and the debate past the data quality stage to look at
analysis, interpretation, and supporting initiatives, because ultimately we are all
working for the well -being of this country.  So it is good information on the state of the
environment that will allow us to fully understand both natural occurrence and the
impact human activities are having.
19 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3375
When we dig a bit deeper and look at the detail of this reporting framework, it is
great to see the different domains that will be reported on. There will be five of them.
There will be air, atmosphere and climate, land, freshwater, and marine. So each of
those domains will be reported on every 6 months, and every 3 years there will be an
integrated report that will inform public and political discussion and debate.
It is great to see the insertion of clauses 6(1A) and 9(2), which will require Ministers
to present reports jointly to the House so that political accountability is encouraged. I
suppose that a key tenet of this National Government is around accountability. That is
our blue -green movement. We have seen today the Greens not supporting this bill,
which would probably represent their red -green movement, but for us it is blue -green. I
know that for an electorate like mine it is very important that we think in this way.
“Waimak” is the third fastest-growing electorate by population growth, but in its history
it is still very much a proud area of primary production. We know that “Waimak” i s like
the rest of New Zealand: when farming is doing well, the whole country does well.
“Waimak” is no different: when farming is doing well, the whole region benefits. With
that primary production, there are risks for the environment, and it will be good  that this
environmental reporting framework will look to ascertain the current data and the
findings around that—the risks of nitrate leaching and the risks of water management.
What we need to do is use reporting like this and use research and innovatio n to
develop and come up with the right solutions to those issues. If we come up with the
right solutions not only will it make our land more productive, which means we will
export more, which means the well -being of this country will continue to grow, but  it
means we will actually have come up with solutions that many other countries are
currently wrestling with or will wrestle with in the future, and that is great for economic
development.
I think that for an asthmatic like me one of the significant doma ins that this reporting
framework will focus on is around air. Two weeks ago was World Asthma Day. We
know that New Zealand has the second -highest rate of asthma in the world: 550,000
schooldays every year are lost because of asthma, 69 deaths in 2011 were  attributed to
asthma, and 7,000 admissions every year in our public hospitals are to do with asthma.
So it is great to see a reporting framework like this. We will be able to tangibly
ascertain the pollution in our airways. I suppose growing up in Christc hurch, which was
synonymous with smog, you would go out for a run in the late evening or in the early
evening and you would wonder whether you were actually doing more damage in going
for the run. But through that we have been able to ascertain by particle s in the air that it
was things around log burners that we have been able to address, and to drive through
the new technology of ultra-low emission burners.
In conclusion, just to recap, you cannot manage what you do not measure. That is
exactly right and this is why we are implementing this legislation. It is great to see that
we will have this legislation and I commend it to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker,
o te rā. Tēnā tātou katoa. It is my honour to take a call on this very important piece of
legislation, the Environmental Reporting Bill 2014. The aim of the bill is to provide for
environmental reports including the type of  information and its quality and timeliness.
When the then Minister for the Environment commented on the first reading of this bill
she stated then that New Zealand was one of only a few OECD countries that did not
require independent reporting on the stat e of the environment. The media release stated
that the scope of the proposed reports will be comprehensive, going beyond the current
non-statutory programme of environmental indicator updates, and would not just cover
the state of the environment but also  describe the pressures driving environmental
3376 Environmental Reporting Bill 19 May 2015
trends and the impact of these trends. Comprehensive information will be provided on
five key environmental domains: air, climate and atmosphere, freshwater, marine, and
land, with biodiversity as a theme acros s all the domains. One of the environmental
domain reports will be released every 6 months and a comprehensive synthesis report
covering all environmental domains will be released every 3 years. I needed to remind
myself of the importance of such a bill.
In this House when we debate legislation we tend to either support or oppose it. As I
stand here, there is almost a third position, which is yes, but not quite. It is fortunate on
the Labour side that we stand opposed to this bill for the very reasons that  my
honourable colleagues Rino Tirikatene and Dr Megan Woods have raised. They were
not raised just from our side, but actually raised in the course of the select committee
hearings, where over 300 submissions made it very, very clear that the issue of thi s
particular legislation is that it does not provide the independence that submitters were
seeking. So I cannot support this piece of legislation because it does not go far enough
in ensuring that the Minister for the Environment is not involved in setting  what those
priority indicators are for both the Government Statistician and the Secretary for the
Environment to report on.
Like I said, over 300 submitters submitted to the select committee process. In Dr
Megan Woods’ contribution to this bill she highl ighted two particular submitters and I
would like to again emphasise what they said. The Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment, Dr Jan Wright, made it clear that the independence issue was critical for
this legislation to have the impact that we a lso desire, which is independent
environmental reporting on issues that make up an important component of our
economy, which is the environment. What did Dr Wright actually say? She made it
really clear that she felt that the bill itself did not offer the level of independence that a
piece of legislation should provide. She made it really clear that she did not think it was
actually a satisfactory function for her to play that role, given her statutory function
within the piece of legislation. What she was seeking was a more independent voice that
set the tone of these reports. So, clearly, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment in her own submission made it clear that more independence was needed
to ensure that this piece of legislation was not interfered with politically.
Another major group that submitted during the submission process was the
Environmental Defence Society, which said: “Allowing Ministers to select topics to be
covered in synthesis reports and domain reports will politicise what should be an
independent process, as topic selection could be utilised to introduce bias into
environmental reporting.” Like I said, many submitted and I wanted to highlight those
particular submitters because of the standing that they have in the env ironmental space,
to ensure that we are putting through legislation that can uphold the very purpose in
which it is being presented to the House.
I want to comment on the Government’s chairperson of the Local Government and
Environment Committee, who, in his debate contribution, made the statement that this
side of the House was opposing a piece of legislation simply for the sake of opposing.
Unfortunately, that is the role of the Opposition —to ensure that all pieces of legislation
that come through this H ouse have gone through the proper process of a select
committee and, more important, has factored in the submissions that were presented to
the select committee. It is concerning that the chairperson of that select committee has
made a statement in terms o f our members who sit on that select committee, who
uphold the submitters who come to the select committee. Yes, as you know, in all select
committees the Government members outnumber the Opposition members, and it has
clearly come through with this piece of legislation coming to the House for this second
19 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3377
reading. What I contend is that unless we acknowledge the importance of the select
committee process in designing robust legislation, we are almost sending a signal to
future submitters that whatever their  concerns or submissions are —and in this case the
majority have asked for independence —this Government is simply not listening. In
terms of coming back to the bill, Labour supports the need for independent
environmental reporting, but the bill falls well s hort of that requirement. It is
fundamentally flawed. Labour is disappointed to oppose this bill, as we believe it is a
vital piece of legislation to protect our environment.
Like earlier mentioned, for too long New Zealand has lagged well behind
international best practice. We are the only country in the OECD without an ongoing
commitment in law to independently and regularly monitor the state of our
environment, so much so that our colleague —again, Dr Megan Woods —in her
contribution offered up Supplement ary Order Paper 74 where she suggests that we
remove the Ministers from making the decision and replace the Ministers with both the
Chief Executive of the Ministry for the Environment and the Government Statistician,
thereby ensuring that there is no politicising and there is no political interference and the
priorities we set for this legislation, in terms of environmental impacts, will be
safeguarded. I really do wish that we had taken that Supplementary Order Paper to heart
when this legislation was comi ng to the House, but it was not to be. It again smacks of
the hidden agendas of this Government, which we are seeing time and time again —a bit
of out of touch; a bit of promising with one hand and taking away with the other.
Can I end by saying that our e nvironment is an important part of who we are as New
Zealanders. We are its guardians, the kaitiaki. What legislation we bring into this House
must guarantee that, at the end of the passing of any legislation, we protect our
environment and that we leave i t in a better state than what we have inherited,
particularly for the future generations. I oppose this bill. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I rise to speak in favour  of the
Environmental Reporting Bill. If I could have the House’s forbearance for perhaps 30
seconds or so, I do want to acknowledge, in the context of local government and
environment, the good work of the Tauranga City Council and staff in response to th e
tornado that hit my electorate late on Thursday. I saw there an example of what actually
happens when you have a natural event of some magnitude and the impact that it has on
individuals and families. It was a very distressing scene amongst a couple of d ozen
homes that were dreadfully affected that Friday morning when I walked around and saw
them all, but by lunchtime most of the obvious effects had been cleaned up and cleared
up. That was a great example of a local government working in tandem with its
community, and I do want to put that on record to acknowledge Tauranga City Council
for what it did there. Well done.
You can also see, actually, the best in community collaboration when it coalesces
around an idea that is supported by good data. I think we  are seeing examples of that
around the country at the moment as various councils reflect on the obligations that
have been imposed on them by the National Policy Statement for Freshwater
Management—a superb piece of reform that this Government brought in over the last
few years that requires real action in respect of water quality improvement. Those
conversations have begun around the country. They are not easy conversations. In many
respects they are quite hard because the data is not complete and there are various trade-
offs that are required to get streams and rivers to mahinga kai - able, to drinkable, to
swimmable. It is very challenging for communities, particularly when they do not have
that full, complete data set, but it is great to see that that is under way.
3378 Environmental Reporting Bill 19 May 2015
It is a real achievement of this Government. I appreciate that there are few on the
other side who would give us any credit for this, but this is a Government that takes a
reform-based approach to managing the environment and that has actually  delivered
outcomes for communities. What we got when we arrived here in 2008 was a complete
vacuum—a vacuum of ideas. There was a vacuum of frameworks and processes to deal
with this. There is shaking of heads on the other side, but you had 9 years to dea l with
this. You are great on rhetoric, but actually putting frameworks in place—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Sorry—the Green Party and Labour are great on rhetoric, but i n
terms of putting frameworks in place that are enduring and that get results, it does not
happen on the other side. It happens on this side, and it is great that the Hon Dr Nick
Smith is in the House today to get some acknowledgment for this side for the reform
agenda that he and Amy Adams have driven through over the last few years.
It is easy to forget that at that time —2008—you could take water without needing to
measure it. There was no National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management. There
were no national objectives frameworks. There was no Land and Water Forum. There
was no framework to enable stakeholders —who only ever saw each other in the
courtroom—to actually sit around a table and say: “How are we going to deal with this?
How are we actually going to progress this debate in a meaningful and enduring way?”,
and that is what this Government, under the leadership of Nick Smith and Amy Adams,
has brought to the table. This is why this Environmental Reporting Bill is so important.
It builds on and continues that 7 years of reform that I touched on.
As my colleague the great Matt Doocey from Waimakariri —what a fantastic MP;
what a great part of the country that is —noted only moments before, we are one of the
few OECD countries that currently does no t require independent reporting, as has been
mentioned, and I think this obviously is going to be redressed shortly with the passing,
hopefully, of this bill. But I do want to make the point that it reflects a party philosophy
on this side of the House aro und progressive transparency. You saw that many decades
ago with the Financial Reporting Act, but —as mentioned by, I think, Nick Smith
himself when he spoke to this bill —an example more recently is the national standards.
We heard it again from Matt Doocey  earlier in terms of the Environmental Protection
Authority, which is an example, and, of course, there are the various Better Public
Services targets that we have in place. This is a party that says that unless you can
measure it, you cannot manage it. So  forget the nice rhetoric —put frameworks in place
that enable you to measure it. Then, from that evidence base, you can drive
improvement forward, and that is what we are doing here in this case. In short, in
respect of this bill, we are not the party of h ollow rhetoric; the other side certainly is,
and I will come back to that shortly.
Essentially, to protect our environment while enjoying and encouraging economic
prosperity, we need to be able to have an honest debate about the interactions between
the environment and the economy, and we need to have a clear picture of the trade -offs
and opportunities that are in place and that are on the table, and of the impacts,
particularly, of the choices that we make. Any argument that presents only half of that
picture is a very undercooked argument indeed. That is why the Environmental
Reporting Bill is so important and is a key piece of the reform agenda that we have
driven in this space, to enable an evidence base to build over time, to enable those
conversations to be deep and have some meaning, so that communities can reach the
right considered outcomes.
I think it is appropriate that we have very clearly specified the domain areas of water
quality, air quality, biodiversity, and of course managing our oceans. Th e approach of
19 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3379
being really specific in terms of the pressures on those particular environments, the
current state of them, and particularly the impacts of various approaches allows you to
take a broader view of these issues. As I have noted, I think this w ill lead to more
informed debate and better options for the public. I think it will be very helpful that we
have the 3 -yearly synthesis reports, to enable some trend analysis. I will touch on that
shortly.
What is very important and has been completely lost in some of the nonsense that we
have heard in this debate over the last half -hour, and certainly a couple of weeks ago, is
that the topics must be selected on the basis of significance, of statistical rigour, of
evidence, and of a strong connection to th e environmental state, and this requires
significant consultation. The debate that we have heard around clause 18, particularly
from the other side, I think is, quite frankly, nonsensical —to hold a view that somehow
it is inappropriate for the Minister for  the Environment to have a view as to what the
topic should be, and, ultimately, through the Cabinet process, sign off what those should
be, particularly when you consider the philosophical underpinning of the parties on the
other side that are suddenly no w talking about the importance of purity and
independence. Every sinew in their political body calls out and cries out to getting
involved in people’s lives. They cannot help it; that is the way their political
philosophies have been built up. It is absolute nonsense.
Sometime in the future, in the mid -2020s, when eventually the Green Party forms a
coalition with New Zealand First and Labour—and will not that be fun—they will stand
over on this side. To think that the Green Party Minister for the Environmen t will not
want to hold a view as to which topic might be covered in an upcoming domain report is
absolute nonsense. From my perspective and from our perspective it is not underpinning
the reality of what is going on here. It is absolutely appropriate for a Minister for the
Environment to hold a view. The changes that have gone on and the various clauses that
we have reflected on to ensure more consultation with iwi and affected local
government talk to a process that has rigour and will deliver the right o utcome for this
country, and not some sort of straitjacket nonsense that we have been having to listen to
over the last half-hour or so.
I do want to spend just a moment, before I conclude, talking about the value of the
synthesis reports, particularly in terms of being able to build up a picture of trends over
time. I am sure that when the first domain reports come out, the reporting will be very
binary. It will be black and white. I suspect on one side all the negative connotations
will be pumped up and p erhaps on the other side we will be talking about the positive
inclinations of what those reports say. But the real value for me is what that will say
over time, because it shows trends in performance and improvement, and trends in
terms of where the press ures are building. If you are really true about building an
environmental picture that can inform public policy and community discussion, then
that is where the value is and that is the value that is inherent in this bill. It deserves
acknowledgment and, in my opinion, deserves support.
In conclusion, I do want to acknowledge the Hon Amy Adams, who started this, and
the Hon Nick Smith, who is concluding it. The rigour of their intellectual—

sections.heading: Reserves And Other Lands Disposal Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I move, That the
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill be now read a second time . It is with great
pleasure that I move the second reading of the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill.
This is an omnibus bill that is provided for in Standing Order 262(1)(e). The intent of
such a bill, which I will refer to as a “ROLD” bill, is to make changes to a land status
that cannot otherwise be dealt with easily. “ROLD” bills deal with authorisations,
transfers, and validations of matters relating to Crown land, reserves, and other lands
held for public or private purposes.  Such bills can be used to correct historic oversights
and errors, or to clarify and simplify issues regarding land status —particularly, when
determining whether a certain use or method of management is legally permissible. The
last “ROLD” bill was enacted  in 2003, and by 2008 sufficient matters had arisen to
warrant this present bill. It is being read again in the House today as a result of a
comprehensive consultation process and thorough consideration of public submissions.
I would like to put on record my thanks to the Primary Production Committee —which,
at the time, was chaired by Shane Ardern —and to all the other members of the
committee who have been involved in progressing the bill to this point.
Among the provisions considered by the committee are several that provide benefits
to communities and community organisations throughout New Zealand. For example,
clauses 38 to 41 of the bill remove a restrictive clause from a 1901 statute and make it
possible for the Dunedin City Council to regularise a lon g-term lease for the use of
reserve land by the Port Chalmers Bowling Club, thus ending many years of uncertainty
for the club. If we go further north, clauses 28 to 34 remove specific hospital -related
purposes and other constraints on five titles for land  held by the Nelson Marlborough
