its Asian Report—I think now it is called Voices. One of my old reporters who used to
work on our television programmes on Television One, Asia Dynamic  and Asia
Downunder, Lynda Chanwai-Earle, does it on Radio New Zealand—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: See, that’s the difference. We’ve got members who’ve done this
stuff.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Yes, she has actually done it. Lynda’s actually a very good
reporter, and she is actually a very good producer, as well.
The kinds of stories that come out on these programmes are —I think there was one
programme she actually did about one of only two co mmissioned officers of the Royal
New Zealand Air Force during the Second World War, who was known as “Willie
McWong”; actually he was William Wong of Dunedin. Those kinds of stories actually
resonate with me, because they tell the stories of the past. I th ink these stories must be
told. When I was doing television, I was very proud to tell the stories of people like
Chew Chong from Taranaki, who was instrumental in the butter export of New Zealand.
He was the first man to block butter and think of exporting  it to England —mother
England. That was the beginning of the dairy industry, and it came from Taranaki and a
Chinese man by the name of Chew Chong. There is even a museum about it in
Taranaki. What I am actually getting at is the sense of national identity  of New Zealand
now. As a nation we are a mix of many ethnicities. I am very proud of the work that
3432 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015
Radio New Zealand does and I hope it will continue to do so in the multi -platform way
that it is able to do.
You know what? As a listener I do not like rad io ads. I do not even like television
ads. I tend to skip them if I can. Often we actually want, as viewers and as listeners, for
Radio New Zealand to produce programmes without commercials. But it does not
actually mean that Radio New Zealand should not b e thinking in a business sense. It
needs to draw more audiences. It needs to be more active in the way that it can actually
draw businesses to support its programmes, not just rely on funding. Do you know,
when I was producing television, television was ve ry expensive to produce. Radio is
too, but I recently went and did an interview with a young man who does podcasting.
When podcasting first started I did not even know what it was, but to think that a
podcast that is generated from Christchurch has listeners from around the world—that is
the modern age of technology, and Radio New Zealand, as an early adopter of
technology, has great advances that it can actually make. I actually commend the work
that the Minister has done. I commend the work that Radio New  Zealand does, and we
actually support it. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Can I just point to some of the opening remarks
that the Minister Amy Adams made in her speech, saying that the intent of this bill from
the Government, the Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill, is to make sure that Radio
New Zealand is relevant, and futureproofing Radio New Zealand. Futureproofing and
keeping Radio New Zealand relevant has been such a priority for this Government that
this piece of legislation was referred to the select committee in June 2009, and it has
languished on the Order Paper through the 49 th Parliament, through the 50 th Parliament,
and it has got to the stage now where the Gove rnment has got hardly anything on the
Order Paper, so this massive priority in public broadcasting has all of a sudden found its
way back on to the Order Paper and it is getting its second reading. Some of the names
on the select committee —some of the memb ers in this House would not even know
who they are. It is two Parliaments ago. This is how much of a priority this Government
is making over public broadcasting.
Such a priority this Government has made over the last 6 years that it has frozen the
budget of Radio New Zealand. Can I just, at this point, make a disclaimer and actually
thank Radio New Zealand and the staff of Radio New Zealand for the work that they
have done under increasingly tight financial conditions. They, as the Minister has said,
are having to tread new waters. The technology is changing, and I will talk about that
later, but Radio New Zealand has got to the stage where it has, at a select committee,
said it has got to the bone and it cannot make any more cuts. So that is the reality of  the
priority that this Government has given public broadcasting.
Let me say, as someone who has actually worked in public broadcasting here and
overseas—I have not had the pleasure of working for Radio New Zealand—that I do not
want Radio New Zealand to b e strong purely for political purposes, for the Labour
Party. I think Radio New Zealand should be strong because there needs to be an
independent journalistic outlet that questions people from all around this House. It
should be coming after all of us, reg ardless of which side of the House we are on. If we
have done something wrong, or done something unpopular, then we need independent
journalism that will take people like us to task. It is absolutely—

items.speaker: Hon Judith Collins
items.text: Absolutely.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Judith. She is going to switch
her vote and come over with us. This is a done deal.
Having independent media is very important, and we support this bill because it sets
out a charter that began its l ife under a Labour Government. But what has happened
over the last 6 years is that, although it is nice to have a charter, the cold, hard reality is
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3433
that this current Government has starved Radio New Zealand of the funding to be able
to do some of the things that are in this piece of legislation. That is one fact. My former
employer, Television New Zealand (TVNZ), which probably is not happy with me since
I have become a member of Parliament because of the criticism that I have poured on it,
has moved from an institution that used to have a charter and a dual remit of being a
public broadcaster and a commercial entity to basically becoming  purely a commercial
entity. I say on the record now that at a select committee hearing not so long ago I asked
the chief executive of TVNZ whether it saw itself as a public broadcaster any more. He
basically said: “No, we’ve got a mandate to make money. That’s all we care about.
That’s what we’re going to do.” On that side of the House that might be OK, but on this
side of the House we do care about some of the tenets of public broadcasting, and one
of those is making sure that you are a participant and making sure that constituents, or
Kiwis, can participate in the democratic process.
I was shocked last week to see a headline in the New Zealand Herald where basically
TVNZ said it did not want any part to play in party political broadcasts any more. The
New Zealand Herald ran that story, and then on the Friday it ran an editorial saying that
it agreed with TVNZ. But the devil  was in the detail there, because basically it wanted
the money that is spent for those party political broadcasts to be spread far and wide,
like to its own newspaper and its own websites. So there is a bit of behind -the-scenes
stuff going on there.
But I actually think that TVNZ, as a State broadcaster, and the likes of Radio New
Zealand, do have an important part to play in a democratic process, whether that is
making sure that constituents, voters, can get the information that they might want in
order to make up their minds on who to vote for, or making sure that there is strong
journalism in New Zealand. I think that what we are seeing at the moment is that it is a
very interesting time in journalism. With the possible cancellation of Campbell Live and
with other changes in journalism, things seem to be getting dumbed down. I am a realist
as well. MediaWorks is a commercial entity; Radio New Zealand is not, and, also,
TVNZ is not. So I think there is an onus on State -owned or public broadcasters to make
sure that they are delivering a decent standard of journalism in New Zealand. And
because of the way that technology is changing, and we are seeing a lot of merging of
media companies at the moment —you will see the New Zealand Herald  and
RadioWorks come to gether to make New Zealand Media and Entertainment —the
standard of journalism is changing. I think that that is a real threat to democracy in New
Zealand and to accuracy, preciseness, in journalism.
So we need to have a standard bearer, and I think that Ra dio New Zealand, and I
hope one day TVNZ in some form of public broadcasting guise, might be able to play
this role. But that is not going to be a reality under the current Government, because
public broadcasting just simply does not seem to be a priority for it. Let us look at its
track record in other areas. TVNZ 6 and TVNZ 7, which were set up by the previous
Labour Government to make sure that State broadcasting had a space in the digital
media, were cut off by Jonathan Coleman, a previous National broadcasting Minister.
I do not hesitate to agree with the Minister that public broadcasters have to change
their game. I do not watch much TV either these days. I have got an internet connection;
I watch Netflix. I watch what I want to watch and when I want t o watch it. But we need
to make sure that New Zealand stories are told and are in that sphere, and if we do not
have a Government that supports the likes of NZ On Air, supports the likes of TVNZ
and local broadcasters and local content producers, and suppo rts Radio New Zealand,
then we are going to be in serious danger of having all this content from around the
world coming into New Zealand and not having any of our own stories to tell. When I
grew up, back in the day, there were lots of New Zealand faces and lots of stories—
3434 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Like what?

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —it was so long ago —out there, whether it be children’s TV or
whether it be documentaries or whether it be factual programmes, as well.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Under the Mountain.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Under the Mountain—no, Terry Teo and things like that, and Video
Dispatch, were very important when I was growing up.
But I think that if we are going into this digital age and we do not have a prioritising
of New Zeala nd content, then I think future generations of New Zealanders will miss
out. We will not have New Zealand stories on air. We will not hear our voices on the
radio. We will get stuff piped in from overseas. Essentially, changes in technology
mean bigger pipes and you can get things faster. One of the first things I said last year
around the changing technologies around broadcasting was that you can have a bigger
pipe, but if you are still sending sewage down it, it is still sewage. Our viewers and our
listeners do not want sewage coming in from overseas. We want good stuff —good
stuff—that is New Zealand made, is our stories, our own voices, and our own people
and our diverse communities in New Zealand, to make sure those stories are being told.
This piece of legislation, in a way, is good, because it started under a Labour
Government that said there needed to be a review and a charter for Radio New Zealand.
There needs to be a review every 5 years. We have already missed one, and we are
likely to have the second miss because of the lateness of this piece of legislation coming
through the House.
So it kind of irks me a little bit to hear the Minister over there saying that they want
to futureproof Radio New Zealand and make sure it is relevant. If they really ca red
about it—and let us be honest, and let us cut to the chase, they do not—they would have
done this a long time ago, and they would not have cut the budget of Radio New
Zealand. They would not have sold off TVNZ 6 and TVNZ 7. They would not have
made TVNZ purely commercial. But it is quite clear that this Government does not care
about public broadcasting.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise and speak on the Radio
New Zealand Amendment Bill. I would like to commend the previous National speaker,
Melissa Lee, and Ms Curran for the very clear passion that they both share. They do not
share the same views, but they clearly both share the same sort of passion for this topic.
Like Mr Faafoi, who has just resumed his seat, I am going to perhaps be a little calmer
and more measured in my views on this, lest people observing this wonder whether
there is some artificial stimulant in the water. I would just like to reassure them that
there is not. This water is homeopathic water. It is merely water diluted by lots of water.
It is very powerful stuff.
Minister Adams, when she introduced the bill in this reading, gave some context as
to where we have come from to get to what we are preparing fo r today. This bill is
about helping Radio New Zealand adapt to technological possibilities and channels and
the opportunities that that creates for today. But looking back gives us some context of
where we have come from, and come so quickly. It was in 192 5 that we first had a
public radio broadcaster. That is 91 years that we have had a public radio broadcaster in
New Zealand. That is a phenomenal achievement when you think of it. Of course, none
of us were there to witness that first day or those early da ys, but we can imagine,
perhaps from stories in our own families over the generations, what it might have been
like—the old wireless technology, valve technology, which had to warm up before it
would work, antenna technology, and reception that was not so great so the signal
would be difficult to hear. It would cut in and out, but people would cluster, families
would cluster, around to hear the news, to be entertained, to learn more about New
Zealand, to learn more about the world. They would get up in the middle of the night, as
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3435
the stories are told, to hear about the All Blacks’ exploits in countries far away, and to
hear the passion of commentators as they described the games, described the points,
described the tries.
And today we have high-definition video. We have very high-quality audio. We have
digital technology for our radio broadcasts, as well. We have not only our traditional
airwaves but the internet as a medium for broadcasting audio, video, and, in fact, written
content. We have so many other  forms of technologies, but at the heart of it, when we
are consuming this —and I will refer specifically to Radio New Zealand content,
whether it is over the airwaves or over the internet —it is still delivering a broadcast of
content that is informing New Zealanders about their communities, their country, the
world and our place in it, and the exploits of New Zealanders in cultural events, in
sports, in business, and in achievements around the globe. It remains as much of a
valuable tool in informing and en tertaining Kiwis and their families as it was 91 years
ago, but it is, if we give it the support, able to do so by leveraging and harnessing the
technological capabilities that are available today. When we look at why this bill is
coming to the House, it i s around this Government’s commitment to delivering Better
Public Services. That includes the continuation of a reliable, independent public radio
capability. In fact, we do not want just to continue that capability; we want to expand
and protect it for th e future, which is why this bill supports Radio New Zealand
expanding into new media platforms and adjusting to changing technological
environments.
As Minister Adams pointed out, there are two core sets of changes in this
amendment. One is a revised char ter, and the second is to make Radio New Zealand
technology-neutral, although I would use slightly different language there because I
would not like to give people the impression that “neutral” in this context is
uninteresting or bland. It is quite the opp osite. In this case, the technology is about
exploiting all of the technological capabilities of the 21 st century—so one that will
exploit web technology and mobile applications, will stream audio, will stream other
content, and will give far more opportunities for Kiwis to be informed.
But let us look first at the Radio New Zealand charter. The charter is a very practical
and pragmatic shift, or reinforcement. It makes a stronger statement about Radio New
Zealand’s role as a public broadcaster. In fact, i n the recent annual review in the
Commerce Committee —in that public hearing, Radio New Zealand reaffirmed its
commitment to a core free -to-air service and no advertising. It also said —and I take a
note, because the members opposite, particularly the previo us Labour speaker, Kris
Faafoi, talked about how dire the circumstances for Radio New Zealand are. The
comment from its chair was that despite difficult circumstances, they, the board, were
confident that they would meet their anticipated budget for the ne xt year. This is a
business that also has to operate in an environment that is close to global financial
crisis. In trying financial circumstances it is delivering more content on more channels
to more people, and its people are saying that they can do it,  and they will do it again
next year. The board, the chief executive officer, and, in fact, the entire team of Radio
New Zealand deserve our congratulations.
Importantly, if the charter is reaffirming Radio New Zealand’s role as a public
broadcaster and a  commercial-free service, the text has been drafted and organised so
that it is more accessible to the public. After all, if this is a public broadcast service it
does make very good sense that the public should be able to understand the charter,
what its intentions are, and how Radio New Zealand will go about delivering that.
I would just like to make a note or two about the select committee process in 2009
when this bill was referred to the Commerce Committee. Unlike 2005, when about 163 -
odd submissions were heard and, despite all of that public interest, despite the clear
3436 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015
interest in the charter revision and the amendment, Labour sat on the bill and did not
bother passing it—despite that public interest, no, it clearly felt that light bulbs and low -
flow shower heads were far more important to New Zealanders than, actually, their
public broadcasting radio service. Well, in 2009 when the bill went before the select
committee for a second time there was a single submission that was made, and that
submission supported the amendments to the charter. But the select committee did not
sit on its hands. It also sought advice from the Ministry for Culture and Heritage and
from the Clerk of the House of Representatives on whether to propose an amendment
that would re quire Radio New Zealand to broadcast summaries of Parliamentary
proceedings.
I can say that that amendment was made in relation to the fact that Radio New
Zealand was no longer making those sorts of broadcasts. The Commerce Committee
was advised that that  was contractually controlled by the Office of the Clerk and,
technically, out of the remit of that particular select committee, but that the broadcaster
may have no editorial input and that would preclude a contract with Radio New
Zealand. Although that is unfortunate for New Zealanders in that it was determined that
they probably would not be able to broadcast these proceedings, we can at least
celebrate that it was reaffirming Radio New Zealand’s right to exercise editorial control
over whatever it is th at it is broadcasting. So the bill was recommended back to the
House by that select committee without amendment.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: When was that?

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: That was in two thousand and—yeah, a few years ago.
What I would like to talk about now is the futureproofing part of this bill. What we
see here is a change and amendment that will support far more web content: webcasting,
audio, video content. But what is really exciting is the launch Radio New Zealand has
had of The Wireless, something that is growing at a phenomenal rate and is really
connecting with other demographics.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: The Green Party supports this bill, and we
absolutely support Radio New Zealand and public broadcasting more generally. There
is nothing really controversial about the bill itself. I suppose the only comment that we
can make is that the Government certainly took a very, very long time to get this bill
before the H ouse. It is not a very complex one. I am not sure why it has taken the
Government so long, but it was required by statute to have a review of Radio New
Zealand’s charter, and that review was undertaken in 2006. It has taken a very, very
long time for this bill to come back to its second reading.
The real problem for Radio New Zealand, and for public broadcasting in New
Zealand generally, is the fact that it is incredibly underfunded. I think the comments
made by Government MPs really gloss over the fact th at we have underfunded public
broadcasting. There has been a funding freeze since 2008. That effectively means there
has been a 10 percent cut to Radio New Zealand since the National Party came into
Government. Of course, it would like to say: “Well, that’ s great. We’re providing the
same great service but we’re spending less money on it.” But it is clear that this is
having an impact on the ability of Radio New Zealand to deliver that important service
to New Zealanders.
In 2007 there was an independent a udit by KPMG that concluded the organisation
was already at that time seriously underfunded, understaffed, and under -resourced. It
recommended an immediate funding increase of $6.7 million. Instead of that, this
National Government has frozen the funding for the 7 years that it is has been in power.
That has clearly had an impact. There have been very high -quality journalists who have
not been able to be retained because they are not able to receive any sort of increase in
salary, despite the fact that costs of living are going up.
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3437
We have a bit of a crisis in public broadcasting because, I believe, the National Party
members do not really believe in public broadcasting, despite what they say. They do
not believe in public broadcasting, they do not really believe in democracy, and yo u can
hear that in their talking points on this bill when they talk about how Radio New
Zealand needs to be more like a business. Well, the purpose of public broadcasting is
not to be commercially viable. The whole purpose of public broadcasting is to prov ide
what the market is not going to provide, and that is independent journalism, which is
essential for citizens in order to have a functioning democracy.
If we look at New Zealand compared with other OECD countries, our level of
funding for public broadc asting per capita is abysmally low. It is almost as low as the
United States, which is, in fact, the only country in this study that spends less on public
broadcasting per capita than New Zealand. I can tell members of this House and those
watching on Parliament TV tonight that public broadcasting is virtually non -existent in
the United States. It is part of the reason we have such a toxic media environment and
such a broken democratic situation in the United States, the country that I come from.
So if we look at other OECD countries and the amount of money that they invest in
public broadcasting, because it is so important and critical to democracy, we can see
that Australia spends three times as much as New Zealand per capita. The UK spends
nearly five times as much per capita. Of course, small countries that are similar in size
to New Zealand —for example, Denmark spends significantly more per capita, about 6
times as much as New Zealand. So New Zealand is falling behind and, of course, it is in
the interest of this National Government to ensure that there is not an independent, well-
funded public broadcaster, because then there will not be anyone there to ensure that the
electorate is hearing in -depth analysis and policy debates. That makes it easier for t his
National Party to get elected when it can rely on superficial branding to get elected and
there is no scrutiny of the actual policy that it is implementing.
The Green Party believes in democracy. We believe in properly funded, independent
public broad casting, not only on radio. We would immediately increase funding to
Radio New Zealand so that it has a proper budget and we would also ensure that there is
proper public broadcasting available on television. We need a non -commercial
television station, wh ich has not occurred since we lost TVNZ 6 and 7. Of course, I
think we need to go a lot further than that if we want to provide quality content and
information. It is not just about news and current affairs, although that is incredibly
important and essent ial to democracy. It is also about entertainment and culture. After
all, we do not want our children in New Zealand growing up with accents like mine. It
is important for New Zealand to preserve its independent identity and it is valuable, I
think, to New Zealanders. I think the National Party is very defensive on this because it
knows that its own voters believe in Radio New Zealand and believe in public
broadcasting. What it would like to get away with is saying it supports these things but
not actually funding them.
The truth is we cannot afford not to have public broadcasting. National would have
you believe we do not have enough money for this; that is like saying we do not have
enough money for elections. If we want a properly functioning democracy we  need a
properly funded public broadcaster both on television and on radio, and if the National
Party—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: How much would you give them? How much?

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: —actually supported Radio New Zealand, then  the
Government would increase the funding by at least the $6.7 million that KPMG
recommended, and, probably, at least indexed to the rate of wage inflation.
I will just conclude by saying that the Green Party wants to see a diverse, quality,
strong, and independent media that contributes to the maintenance of effective
3438 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015
democracy and Aotearoa New Zealand’s social, cultural, economic, and environmental
well-being. This National Party understands the cost of many things, but the value of
very few. Thank you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: It has been an interesting debate
while I have been sitting in the House, particularly the interaction between the
Government members and the Labour Party members, trying to figure out who took the
longest to get nowhere.
I just want to quote a few statements with regard to this particular bill. This is what
has been said previously about this bill: “ This bill languished under the last
administration, whereas this Government is committed to fulfilling i ts legislative
responsibilities.” It just never got around to doing it. “ This is an unfair situation for
Radio New Zealand, and it shows that the previous Minister [of Broadcasting] had other
priorities. It is highly desirable that the related legislative process be concluded as soon
as possible to ensure that Radio New Zealand can operate to an up -to-date and clear
public service mandate. The adoption into legislation of the revised charter supports this
Government’s manifesto commitment to provide certainty in relation to the operations
of public service broadcasters.” Those quotes were from the Minister of Broadcasting at
the time, the Hon Dr Coleman, of the National Government, back in 2009.
Members on the Government benches have made much of the fact that the original
review around the content of the charter was made in 2005, with 135 submissions at the
time, and that the Commerce Committee at that time considered those submissions and
then came up with a few tweaks and so on for the charter. It then came back to this
House, which then needed to be turned into legislation, which then went back to the
Commerce Committee.
So there has been much made by the National Government members in an attempt to
override what they knew was going to be a drumming when they came into this House
with this bill. The reason why they were going to get a drumming —and they knew it—
was that those statements were made in 2009 about how important this piece of
legislation was, and they were made by the Minister about how terrible it was that it had
been left for 3 years and nothing had happened. And now here we are 6 years later
under a National Government looking at the same piece of legislation, which,
fascinatingly, eve n though it has changed almost not a jot since 2009, is now
apparently—according to the speakers from the Government benches —going to
completely update and modernise Radio New Zealand for the new digital age and for
the many media platforms that are available now.
That is a miracle. It is a miracle that when something just sits on the Order Paper for
6 years it suddenly becomes the answer for the future. Maybe we should just leave
everything on the Order Paper and then eventually it will morph itself into the future.
Well, that would be lovely but you know, like I know, Mr O’Connor, that that is not
going to happen.
But let us just take some other quotes. This speaker on this bill said the following: “I
commend Dr Coleman for his courage to take action ove r this bill, a bill that was an
example of the Labour Party resting on its laurels and not getting legislation through
this House. It is a brave move by Dr Coleman to take this legislation on and move it
quickly through the House.” So what happened to that  courage, which started in 2009
and now we are here in 2015? What happened—

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: We got busy.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: What happened, Mr Bishop? What happened to the courage?
Did all the courage leave the House when the members of the original Commerce
Committee that looked at this bill left? Is that what happened, Mr Bishop? There is no
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3439
more courage left to drive such i mportant legislation through this House, and that is
why it has spent 6 years sitting on this Order Paper?
It fascinates me that we have had National Party members stand and passionately
argue how important—how important—public broadcasting service is for New Zealand.
And it absolutely is. New Zealand First absolutely agrees that there must be an
independent, non -commercial public broadcaster for New Zealand. We agree and we
believe, as the Green Party spokesperson said, that there should be a public broadcasting
non-commercial television station. Ms Collins holds her head in her hands —now she
sits on the Education and Science Committee. What a shame she was not on the
committee when she was a Minister because she would have heard her Government
members on that select committee at the time also raving and being very passionate
about Learning Media and its opportunity to create digital content in visual and in radio
form that would retain the voice of New Zealand across our public service radio. But
Miss Coll ins was not there and now holds her head in her hands in a back seat,
backbench position.
Of course, what happened was that this Government on the one hand said that this
was a wonderful thing and Learning Media had this opportunity and could keep the
New Zealand voice there for New Zealanders. Then the Government drove it out of
business by opening Learning Media up to 100 percent competition while at the same
time it had its hands tied behind its back with regard to what it had to provide for the
Government for free.
So it is fascinating to listen to the Government members stand and argue how much
they believe in public broadcasting, and how much they believe that this institution
should remain and should be well funded. They have not funded it properly for the last
7 years, but today, after 6 years of this being on the Order Paper —so Radio New
Zealand not technically having a legal charter, or at least not a charter that has been
reviewed in the modern age, and not increasing its funding in any other way—they have
decided that it is incredibly important and that they must push it through.
It will be interesting to see what is in the Budget. Is there any money, Mr Bishop, in
the Budget for Radio New Zealand? Is there any money, Mr Bishop? Will you finally
give public broadcasting money? After all the statements made, will that Government
finally give public broadcasting any more money?

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Wait and see. It’s a good Budget.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Is that a no, Mr Bishop? Is that a no? Is that a no, Mr Bishop?

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: It’s a good Budget. It’s a good Budget, Tracey.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: That is a no. There you go. So, unfortunately, for Radio New
Zealand and those pe ople in New Zealand who believe in public broadcasting, do not
look to this Government to try to fund it appropriately. They will talk the talk in the
middle of night. They will talk the talk, but they will not walk the walk. So do not
expect anything inside this Budget.
The only other thing that New Zealand First would say is that it is incredibly
important that we keep an independent voice, but is Radio New Zealand currently as
independent and informative as it should be for the New Zealand public? I thi nk one
needs to go and have a look, and we challenge the broadcaster itself to go and have a
look. Is it unbiased in its political reporting, for example? Does it gain comment from
across the whole of the political spectrum on issues that are of importance?
We would challenge it to go and have a look at the percentages of its reporting and
the percentage of comment that it seeks from political party spokespersons on issues
that are of importance —important enough for it to put on the radio station and make
programmes about, such as the Trans -Pacific Partnership. It appears to be picking and
choosing political parties in order to gain a bias. New Zealand First would argue that
3440 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015
there are voices in the political arena that New Zealanders need to hear on issues like
the Trans-Pacific Partnership, on issues like foreign investment, and on issues that this
Government has been trying to push through again and again through a
misrepresentation to the New Zealand people.
We would suggest that it is not only timely fo r this organisation to have its charter
passed through here so that it can actually provide comprehensive, independent,
accurate, impartial, and balanced regional, national, and international news and current
affairs. We would encourage it to seek comment from every political party inside this
House on a regular basis and in an apolitical manner.
Do not be frightened of the National Government. Make sure that you keep in the
charter comments that are here in the charter. We would absolutely support that th is bill
needs to be passed now so that Radio New Zealand can actually get on with its business.
We also would support that if there are any crumbs left in the Budget, Mr Bishop,
perhaps we could throw a few to Radio New Zealand. Otherwise, New Zealand Firs t
joins with the other Opposition parties in saying that we actually believe in public
broadcasting and we would fund it to the level it should be appropriately funded at.

items.speaker: Hon JUD ITH COLLINS
items.text: What a joy to follow that
member, Tracey Martin, who has just resumed her seat. Everything from now on has to
be better, does it not, really? I mean, for goodness’ sake! Let me take up the cudgels on
behalf of Radio New Zea land after that horrible attack from New Zealand First. Radio
New Zealand should be able to put on commentary from the politicians whom it wants
to hear from, not the ones it is made to hear from—good on Radio New Zealand.
I would like to take up a point that Kris Faafoi made. He said that we had no
commitment to Radio New Zealand. Well, actually, I remember 1YA —of course, I was
a child at the time —and we had this fabulous programme on Sunday mornings called
Flick the Little Fire Engine . That was Radio New  Zealand when I was growing up, and
I think it is still on, actually, in some parts. It is the same programme over and over
again, which is pretty fantastic —it is called recycling. But, really, we have $35 million
worth of taxpayer money of commitment—
Simon O’Connor: How much?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: $35 million every year going to Radio New Zealand. If I
tell you how much taxpayer money goes to Newstalk ZB—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: Zero.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Zero. How much goes to Radio Live? Hmm —zero. How
much goes to Radio Hauraki? Zero. How much goes to Classic Hits? Zero. How much
goes to the Breeze—my favourite station, personally, because it plays good music when
I am driving? Zero. That is it—zero—and yet we have $35 million a year of taxpayer
money going to Radio New Zealand. I think that is money well spent, myself. I just love
being interviewed by Mary Wilson on Checkpoint. Nothing gets better than that. There
is nothing like that, with t he sort of rabid interviewer coming down through the line,
ripping your heart out—fantastic stuff. Then there is Morning Report—unfairly, I think,
referred to occasionally as “Moaning Report”. That is very unfair, because I actually
really enjoy listening to Susie Ferguson and Guyon Espiner. I challenge New Zealand
First—and Tracey Martin, the deputy leader —to come up with one reason why they
would want to interview New Zealand First.
Radio New Zealand has a very balanced view. It is not always fond of the
Government, especially when it is us. But, having said that, I still think Radio New
Zealand is in a really good place to be. They are, in fact, the people who do not have to
get advertising to pay their wages, unlike every other radio station with whom t hey
compete. They have an obligation to produce something that we expect, which is sound,
balanced radio. Occasionally they get it wrong. I was listening to The Panel one day just
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3441
last week when that lovely Jim Mora, whom I am very fond of, had on that lad y—you
know, she is the one who does those baking soda cleansers. She was commenting —I
have no idea why —along with somebody else, similarly left wing. They were
commenting in a really balanced way: all left. I thought: “Well, isn’t that great?”. I
thought t hat, actually, the public can listen to this and they will make up their own
minds. But do you know what? Radio New Zealand, apart from all that —and we all
have our little sorts of things about it—I actually think generally does a really good job.
Kris Faafoi said we are not interested in public broadcasting. Well, yes, we are. He
also wondered why Television New Zealand does not want to run all these TV political
ads at election time. I will tell you why. Mostly, they are really boring; mostly, they
really are. When Mr Assistant Speaker and I were growing up —well, he was growing
up a lot earlier than me, I have to say—there was not any choice. People, basically, were
chained to the TV —the one station, and at one stage, the two stations —waiting for the
little kiwi to come out at about 9.30 p.m. to tell us to go to bed. That is what it was like.
I know Dr Megan Woods is looking at this and saying: “Is this true?”. It was. Worse
than that, it was in black and white. That is actually what we used to have with o ur
public broadcasting dollar.

items.speaker: But let us just wonder this
items.text: why do we have public broadcasting? Actually we had it,
to start with, because there was no commercial interest or ability to bring it about. But I
think it has actually won a place in people’s h earts. Where else is one going to learn
about bird calls, other than Radio New Zealand? That is a good thing. Should you wake
up at 5 o’clock in the morning, for some strange reason, and need to go back to sleep,
what else are you going to do? Turn on Radi o New Zealand at 5 o’clock in the morning
and you will go back to sleep. It is fantastic. But I am digressing. The fact is that Radio
New Zealand has $35 million of taxpayer money every single year. That is $35 million
more than every other radio station t hat it competes with. I actually think that is quite a
good deal, frankly. If I were Radio New Zealand I would be pretty pleased with that.
I would also like to say that I actually think Radio New Zealand has really improved
its performance around communicating with, and making itself accessible to, the public.
As we have heard, from all the speakers tonight, everyone is saying they have thing s
like Netflix and stuff like that. Well, actually, I do not. I generally try to watch some
television—normally not the news, because it is always a bit dull and depressing; I
actually like seeing ordinary TV, occasionally. But do you know what? We have so
much more choice nowadays. So many of the Radio New Zealand programmes are
really good. If you cannot listen to them at the time, then you can listen to them on the
internet later on. It has a very good service on the internet, so that it is very quickly
available. If you want to go and check your interview, what has happened, what is going
on with something, or what the bird call was for today, it is actually available, and I
think that is important. That is no different, by the way, from the commercial s tations
with which they compete.
But I will say Radio New Zealand has certain obligations. For instance, its leaders
come to our Commerce Committee and report to us every year on their annual review.
They come to us to talk about what they have done with the $35 million that they get
every year—more than every other radio station and broadcaster. They tell us what they
are doing. I was really pleased this year to be able to say to the Radio New Zealand
board, when they turned up with the chief executive, t hat I think they are doing a great
job. I know it is a lot of money. It is actually a huge amount of money. But having said
that, Radio New Zealand is something that a lot of people listen to. I am one of those
people who listen to it during the day if I h ave a chance to. But, then again, I also listen
to Newstalk ZB.
3442 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015

19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3357 
 
TUESDAY, 19 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
ORAL QUESTIONS  
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Budget 2015—Economic Programme 
1. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: How will Budget 2015 
progress the Government’s commitment to manage the Government’s finances, while 
delivering better public services? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : We will follow the same approach of 
stable and predictable management of the Government’s finances, with the objective of 
better public services for New Zealanders. We know that this is working because there 
are today 42,000 fewer children living in benefit-dependent households than 3 years ago 
and 194,000 new jobs compared with 4 years ago. Core Crown e xpenditure this year 
will be around $4 billion lower than we thought it would be back in 2011. These 
changes are making a real difference to people’s lives. 
Chris Bishop: How will Budget 2015 help New Zealanders and their families? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The member will have to wait until Budget day to see the 
whole plan , but we  have already made some announcements that will benefit New 
Zealand families. ACC levy cuts will bring about $500 million worth of savings to New 
Zealanders. We have announced $98 million for more timely elective surgery and 
improved orthopaedic treatment and also $32 million to strengthen compliance with 
minimum employment standards. And we are putting $33 million towards more 
immigration officers because New Zealand is such a success story that we are getting 
more visitors, migrants, and tourists and need more capacity at the border. 
Chris Bishop: What other Budget 2015 decisions have been announced? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : We ar e providing the Inland Revenue Department with an 
additional $29 million for greater property tax compliance. We already tax the gain that 
people make when they sell a property that they bought with the intention of reselling it, 
and that is fair. We are s harpening up those rules to make it easier for the Inland 
Revenue Department to enforce them and help ensure that people understand their 
liabilities. So everyone will have to provide their IRD number on every property they 
buy, other than their main home,  and everyone will know there will be a 2 -year 
brightline test, meaning that gains from property sold within 2 years of purchase will be 
taxed, except if it is the main place of residence, or inherited, or part of a matrimonial 
settlement. 
Grant Robertson: Does he recall saying in the 2014 Budget speech “There will be a 
small surplus next year , and increasing surpluses are forecast over time.” , and now, 
having broken that promise, will he be using exactly the same sentence in this year’s 
Budget speech? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I do remember making that statement as part of the 2014 
Budget, and it indicated significant progress from an $18 billion deficit to what will turn 
out to be a $500 million or $600 million deficit. It falls short of the surplus that was 
budgeted by a bit, and that means we will achieve surplus next year. 
Chris Bishop: What particular measures in Bu dget 2015 apply to property investors 
who may be based overseas? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: As well as having to supply a New Zealand IRD number, all 
non-resident—that is, non - tax resident—buyers and sellers must also provide their tax 
3358 Oral Questions  19 May 2015 
 
ID number from their home country, along with a current ID such as a passport. This 
will enable the Inland Revenue Department to share tax information with overseas 
authorities. Also, to ensure that our full anti  - money-laundering rules apply to non -
residents, they must have a New Zealand bank account before they get a New Zealand 
IRD number. Finally, we will be looking at introducing a withholding tax for non - tax 
residents, which, if adopted, means we will take the tax off immediately when the 
property is sold, and the foreign owner will have to square up with the Inland Revenue 
Department later. 
Andrew Bayly: How does the increased compliance on property gains fit within the 
Government’s response to escalating Auckland house prices? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The real issue in Auckland is that there are too few houses to 
meet demand. So the problem is pretty simple, but ensuring more supply is the most 
effective long-term tool for bringing some order to the Auckland property market. So 
we are working on a number of fronts: changes in the tax regime, which may dampen 
demand; setting up special housing areas to free up more land; and concentrating on 
redeveloping extensive Government landholdings in Auckland —for instance, 
transferring Housing New Zealand properties to the Tāmaki Redevelopment Company. 
Andrew Bayly: How do those decisions sit within the Government’s commitment to 
control its spending? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : These commitments are all being financed by  a relatively 
low level of new Government initiatives. So, for instance, the total annual cost of new 
initiatives in this Government’s last six Budgets is around $3 billion. The last six 
Budgets of the previous Government had $20 billion of new initiatives , and at the end 
of that time, even supporters of it, such as the Salvation Army, were led to conclude that 
despite all the spending, there were no better outcomes for New Zealand communities. 
With less new spending we are getting better outcomes. 
Housing Market—Auckland 
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement that there is no housing crisis in Auckland in light of the fact the  
average Auckland house price has risen by $100,000 in the past year and the Reserve 
Bank says this is “increasing the risk of financial instability”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, because over the last few years I have 
heard many overstated claims of a crisis in various parts of the economy. The previous 
one was apparently in manufacturing. The Government and the Reserve Bank have both 
acknowledged that we need more houses bui lt in Auckland and we need to make that 
happen faster. That is why the Government has taken significant action to increase 
supply and speed up land development. 
Andrew Little: Why has he introduced a measure that looks like a capital gains tax, 
but which he says is not one, to fight an Auckland property market that is in crisis, but 
which he says is not? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Just to quote Mr Little, he said the policy is “not a capital 
gains tax”. What we have done is said that  for anyone who is an investor in a 2 -year 
period, we will take the ambiguity out of the current situation because we believe that 
that is reasonable. And for foreigners whom we do not have good records on in New 
Zealand—yes, they will be forced to pay their fair share of tax. 
Andrew Little: In light of his finance Minister’s comment that it is “a bit unclear” 
what impact his new measures will have, by how much does he say the new brightline 
test will slow the growth of Auckland house prices; and if he does not know, why not? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, we have not modelled that, but what I can say is that, of 
the additional money we are putting into inspectors —which is $29 million in this 
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3359 
 
Budget and $33 million from Budget  2013, which is yet to be spent; that is $62 
million—the expectation is that we will get $420 million. The reason we are likely to 
get at least $420 million, if not more, is that the ambiguity is removed. I will say, 
though, that the intention test has bee n around for a very long period of time. Funnily 
enough, and I have not actually bothered to go and look at it, if one was to go back and 
look at all the advice that the previous Labour Government got when house prices 
doubled under its watch, one would pr obably look at this issue as an issue that was 
raised back then. But guess what? Labour did nothing; National acts. 
Andrew Little: How many property speculators who are not already caught by the 
intention test will be caught by the brightline test; and if he does not know, why not? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The analysis of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and 
Employment suggests that between 17 and 18 percent of Auckland’s housing 
transactions currently involve houses being boug ht and sold within 2 years. I would be 
pretty surprised if all of those owners are paying tax on that, and I would strongly 
suggest that quite a few more will as a result of the brightline test. 
Andrew Little : Why has he announced a tax pol icy when he does not know how 
well it will work, whom it will catch, or what the rules even are? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I know whom it will catch, and they are people who buy and 
sell an investment property within 2 years. They are foreigners w ho are currently non - 
resident income taxpayers who are not paying their fair share of tax. Yes, the 
Government takes a careful and cautious approach in this regard, but that is the right 
thing to do because, in the end, taxpayers are entitled to have som e clarity in what they 
are doing. But I do think, and the Government has thought this for quite a long period of 
time, that the intention test needs reflecting upon, and that was the very reason why we 
asked the Inland Revenue Department to look at this ve ry issue back in 2010. The 
officials in 2010 said they did not think we should move on it; in 2015 they changed 
their minds. 
Andrew Little: Why will he not just be straight with New Zealanders and admit that 
his new policies will not fix th e Auckland housing crisis, and that he is just doing the 
bare minimum and hoping the problem will go away because he does not have a clue 
what to do? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Under this Government we have special housing areas of 
which there are about 90 in Auckland. Under this Government we have reduced the 
duty on imported materials. Under this Government we have reformed the Resource 
Management Act, and we are looking to do more. Under this Government we have 
introduced a new brightline test fo r those who buy and sell investment properties. We 
have done a lot in the housing area. I know that Labour members do not like it, but 
house prices doubled under their watch. Actually, Auckland house prices went up by 79 
percent under the previous Labour G overnment. When they asked Andrew Little last 
week what—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER : Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Prime Minister will resume his 
seat. 
Housing Market—Overseas Buyers 
3. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does 
he stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Does he stand by the following statements: in May last 
year, “There is no housing crisis in Auckland.”; also in May last year, “I do not believe 
there is a crisis in housing.”; in June last year, “It’s not a crisis.”; in April this yea r, “So 
3360 Oral Questions  19 May 2015 
 
I don’t think you could call it a crisis.”; and just last month, “I don’t believe a capital 
gains tax works.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes, I stand by all of those statements. Interestingly enough, if 
you look at the information by the Re al Estate Institute, figures across New Zealand 
actually show that although Auckland house prices are up, the rest of the country is very 
mixed; some are actually down. And, interestingly enough, if you look at the equivalent 
period of time under the last Labour Government, house prices doubled. Under National 
they have gone up nationally by 35 percent. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Does he stand by this statement, made by himself: “I don’t 
believe foreigners buying the odd house in New Zealand is what’s driving the escalation 
of prices”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, I believe that statement is correct. I think that there is 
quite a degree of confusion, actually, about the people who buy houses in New Zealand, 
who may come from ove rseas originally or may not be Caucasian. But I think the 
number of very large purchases of properties in New Zealand that are from offshore is 
likely to be quite a low number—lower than what people expect, in my view. 
Rt Hon Winston  Peters: Does he agree with Lyndon Fairbairn of All Property —
[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Will the Leader of the House contain himself. Will the 
member please start his supplementary question again. 
Rt Hon Winston Pe ters: Does he agree with Lyndon Fairbairn of All Property 
Solutions, who, when asked on Morning Report this morning whether the Government’s 
measures will be strenuous on foreign buyers, replied “No, not at all.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : That is  an interesting view that the gentleman might have —
and I do not know who he is. But let us put it this way. If the rules are, as they will be, 
that a foreign buyer or a non - resident taxpayer—because that is the test, actually, a non 
- resident tax status —has to provide their IRD number, has to provide a New Zealand 
bank account, and, by the way, by the middle of next year will have withholding tax 
taken off any sales of properties, and they will then have to reverse the burden to get 
that tax back. If that is no effect, then that is a very interesting world that that gentleman 
lives in, but I would suggest it is one that is quite a long way away from reality. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Why does he not just stop tinkering around the edges  and, 
to use his words, “get some guts” and back New Zealand buyers, and stop foreign non -
residents buying New Zealand land and houses? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : We know Mr Peters’ views about foreign investment and the 
likes into New Zealand. But , interestingly enough, maybe the member, when he returns 
back to his office for a nice cup of tea this afternoon, might want to have a look on the 
Sydney Morning Herald website, where they actually talk quite openly about how house 
prices are rising much faster there than they are in Auckland. And the article goes on to 
say: “It would be nice if there was a single guilty party —foreigners, investors, negative 
gearing, local Government, capital gains discounts, cheap money, population growth —
but it’s much more complicated” than all of those. 
Child Support—Reforms 
4. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of 
Finance: Does he stand by his statement that “we believe the strong underlying 
economy and responsible fiscal management can deliver a surplus when the final 
Government accounts are published next October”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Financ e): I stand by my full statement made at 
the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, which was: “falling dairy prices and low 
inflation are restricting growth in the nominal economy and Government revenue. This 
19 May 2015 Oral Questions  3361 
 
makes it more challenging for the Government to  achieve surplus in 2014-15. However, 
we remain on track to reduce debt to 20 per cent … by 2020. Although this latest 
Treasury forecast predicts a small deficit for the current year, we believe the strong 
underlying economy … can deliver a surplus when th e final Government accounts are 
published next October,”. 
Grant Robertson: Can he explain to the House how it is an example of “responsible 
fiscal management” to allow a blowout in expenditure from $34 million to $210 million 
for the upgrade of the Child Support system at the Inland Revenue Department? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The member may want to delve into the details of that. As I 
recall it, at least a fair bit of the expenditure came from two sources. One was that the

RESERVES AND OTHER LANDS DISPOSAL BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Land Information) : I move, That the 
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill be now read a second time . It is with great 
pleasure that I move the second reading of the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill. 
This is an omnibus bill that is provided for in Standing Order 262(1)(e). The intent of 
such a bill, which I will refer to as a “ROLD” bill, is to make changes to a land status 
that cannot otherwise be dealt with easily. “ROLD” bills deal with authorisations, 
transfers, and validations of matters relating to Crown land, reserves, and other lands 
held for public or private purposes.  Such bills can be used to correct historic oversights 
and errors, or to clarify and simplify issues regarding land status —particularly, when 
determining whether a certain use or method of management is legally permissible. The 
last “ROLD” bill was enacted  in 2003, and by 2008 sufficient matters had arisen to 
warrant this present bill. It is being read again in the House today as a result of a 
comprehensive consultation process and thorough consideration of public submissions. 
I would like to put on record my thanks to the Primary Production Committee —which, 
at the time, was chaired by Shane Ardern —and to all the other members of the 
committee who have been involved in progressing the bill to this point.  
Among the provisions considered by the committee are several that provide benefits 
to communities and community organisations throughout New Zealand. For example, 
clauses 38 to 41 of the bill remove a restrictive clause from a 1901 statute and make it 
possible for the Dunedin City Council to regularise a lon g-term lease for the use of 
reserve land by the Port Chalmers Bowling Club, thus ending many years of uncertainty 
for the club. If we go further north, clauses 28 to 34 remove specific hospital -related 
purposes and other constraints on five titles for land  held by the Nelson Marlborough 
District Health Board. That change will enable the board to make more effective use of 
the land when providing health and disability support services to the Nelson -
Marlborough community. And in Northland, clauses 21 to 23 fo rmalise a community -
supported agreement that reserve land in Māhinepua Bay be vested as a Māori 
reservation with the trustees of the adjoining Māori reservation. 
Shortly I want to go through two substantive changes to the bill, but, first, I would 
like to comment on a general issue that was raised during the select committee process, 
and which is referred to specifically in the Primary Production Committee’s 
commentary on the bill. An overriding issue, which arose in discussions on a number of 
clauses in the bill, is whether applications that could be considered controversial should 
be included in a “ROLD” bill. The convention is for “ROLD” bills to deal with non -
controversial matters. However, several applications —and two examples are the 
Auckland City Coun cil’s application relating to Albert Park and the Department of 
Conservation’s application relating to land adjoining Auckland’s volcanic cones —were 
considered by some to be controversial. The committee questioned whether a “ROLD” 
bill was the appropriate legislative vehicle for some of these issues. The committee felt 
19 May 2015 Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill 3381 
 
it was being asked, effectively, to rubber -stamp what were controversial issues, and it 
questioned whether or not councils may view the bill as an opportunity to avoid other 
difficult and time-consuming legislative processes. This is a matter that Parliament may 
wish to consider. However, it is worth noting that the convention that “ROLD” bills 
deal with non -controversial land matters was intended to ensure that changes remain 
technical. The r eality is that most of the changes in this bill as reported back by the 
committee are technical changes that deal only with administrative and technical details. 
The Primary Production Committee recommended two substantive changes to the 
bill. The first wa s the result of a decision by the Department of Conservation to 
withdraw its application relating to the Sugar Loaf Islands in New Plymouth. The 
committee has recommended that clauses 42 to 44, which relate to this application, be 
deleted. This change had the consent of all parties involved, and I am comfortable with 
the removal of these clauses. I believe the committee has also recommended the 
insertion of clauses 34A, 34B, and 34C, which deal with a parcel of esplanade reserve 
land at Ōpua in the Bay of I slands. I believe the committee acted with good intentions 
when it recommended the insertion of these clauses; however, I do not believe they are 
suitable for inclusion in the bill. To that end I intend, during the Committee stage, to 
move a Supplementary Order Paper seeking their deletion, and I will provide detail of 
that in the Committee of the whole House. 
I will also seek your support during the Committee stage for a number of other 
proposed amendments. Most of these are of minor and technical nature. For example, 
updates are required to reflect the changes in Auckland local government that have 
taken place since the committee reported the bill back to Parliament. Clause 5, which 
amends the Reserves Act 1977, is to be deleted because the matters dealt w ith by this 
clause have since been resolved by the statutes amendment legislation that was recently 
enacted in this House. Technical amendments are also proposed to clauses 21 to 23, 
which, as I mentioned earlier, formalise a community -supported agreement to have an 
area of esplanade reserve at Māhinepua Bay in Northland declared a Māori reservation. 
These amendments clarify the process to be followed to achieve this aim. Clauses 18 to 
20, concerning Waitaki District Council’s application regarding Lookout Point, are to 
be deleted. These clauses are no longer required because the matter they deal with has 
been resolved by the Waitaki District Council Reserves and Other Lands Empowering 
Act. I also intend to recommend the deletion of clauses 10 to 11, which c oncern 
decision making for earthworks on Auckland volcanic cones, and clauses 24 to 27, 
which concern Marlborough District Council land in Picton. I have made this 
suggestion in order to allow further consultation with interested parties. 
I wish to make a few final comments on one of the provisions mentioned in the 
committee’s report. Clauses 6 to 9 enable a technical change to the status of a parcel of 
land in Albert Park, which has been designated as a local purpose art gallery reserve. 
This change is adm inistrative and amends the definition of Albert Park in Auckland 
City for this purpose. The provisions in the bill enable the amalgamation of land in 
Albert Park with the adjacent parcel of freehold land, which the gallery sits on. Having 
both parcels on t he same title will avoid costly and time -consuming administrative 
issues. The committee’s report outlines the concerns that some members shared with 
submitters who were opposed to the expansion of the gallery. Submitters were under the 
impression that the “ROLD” bill was enabling what they viewed as an alienation of 
reserve land in Albert Park. In a technical and legal sense, the clauses in the “ROLD” 
bill were not enabling any alienation. The former Auckland City Council reclassified 
the relevant land as l ocal purpose art gallery reserve land in accordance with the 
Reserves Act 2006. The council submitted a notice of requirement for a designation 
under the Resource Management Act 1991, which was approved by the Environment 
3382 Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill 19 May 2015 
 
Court in August 2008. Resource con sents for works within Albert Park not covered by 
the designation were also granted by the Environment Court in its 2008 decision. It was 
these processes that gave the council the necessary authority to proceed with the 
expansion of the gallery.  
Members o f the committee acknowledged that there had not been any technical 
alienation; however, they felt that although the council had followed due process and 
was within its legal rights to begin the gallery expansion, the park was originally 
classified as recre ational reserve with the intention that the land be preserved as open 
space. The Primary Production Committee did not approve of the city council’s 
approach to dealing with this matter, and I do have some sympathy with its view. 
However, any problematic is sues with the gallery development occurred in processes 
beyond the scope of this bill. The clauses in the “ROLD” bill will prevent Auckland Art 
Gallery management from having to deal with unnecessary administrative difficulty in 
operating the gallery as it  is. This will benefit all Auckland ratepayers by enabling the 
efficient and effective management of an important cultural and entertainment resource. 
The provisions in this bill will give effect to applications by local authorities and 
Government agencies  for technical changes to land status that remove administrative 
and technical barriers that would otherwise prevent owners and lessees from effectively 
and efficiently managing and administrating the land. I commend this bill to the House.

3402 Standards and Accreditation Bill 19 May 2015 
 
STANDARDS AND ACCREDITATION BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs) : I 
move, That the Standards and Accreditation Bill be now read a second time . The 
purpose of the bill is to ensure New Zealand’s standards and conformance system is 
viable and well functioning and meets the needs of business, regulators, and consumers 
into the foreseeable future. The bil l achieves this by putting in place new arrangements 
for New Zealand standards development and approval and by updating the institutional 
arrangements for the Testing Laboratory Registration Council to better reflect the nature 
of its functions. The bill b rings together the law relating to standards and accreditation 
of conformity assessment bodies, and it repeals and replaces the Standards Act 1988 
and the Testing Laboratory Registration Act 1972.  
The new arrangements for standards include the establishme nt of the New Zealand 
Standards Approval Board and the New Zealand Standards Executive. The board will 
approve New Zealand standards and membership of standards development committees 
and advise the responsible Minister on the currency of New Zealand stand ards, the 
priority areas for the development of New Zealand standards, and the review of existing 
New Zealand standards. The Standards Executive will be an independent statutory 
officer located in the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. The St andards 
Executive will be responsible for standards development and will assume responsibility 
for New Zealand’s membership of the International Organization for Standardization 
and the International Electrotechnical Commission. These new arrangements will  
replace the Standards Council, which will be disestablished.  
I have heard the concerns regarding the independence of the standards system. 
Stakeholders can be assured that this has been a key consideration in the development 
of the new arrangements. The Standards Approval Board and the Standards Executive 
are statutorily independent. Neither is subject to the direction of Ministers. The board 
will be guided by decision-making criteria in the legislation when considering proposed 
standards and proposed mem bership of standards development committees. The 
Standards Executive will be required by the legislation to continue the practice of 
developing standards by using independent committees of technical experts approved 
by the board, reflecting an expectation of international and domestic standards 
communities. I am confident that these and other measures will continue to support the 
independence of the standards system. I also note that there are a number of different 
institutional models for standards around the world, including where the standards 
development function is located within the Government agency.  
The current cost recovery model for standards will be strengthened by this bill. The 
bill provides a framework to allow the Standards Executive to enter  into arrangements 
that cover the life cycle of standards, balancing initial development and approval costs 
with ongoing costs for maintenance and access. This will provide a sustainable financial 
footing for the standards system—a key driver for change.  
In relation to accreditation, the bill updates the provisions of the Testing Laboratory 
Registration Act 1972 to reflect the contemporary nature of the functions of the Testing 
Laboratory Registration Council that relate to accreditation of testing and ins pection 
services. The bill will also rename the council as the Accreditation Council.  
I commend the Commerce Committee for producing useful commentary in only 4 
months and I thank those who submitted on the bill for their contribution. The 
committee’s ana lysis of submissions has resulted in a number of sensible 
recommendations. I am pleased to say that the bill has been amended to provide a more 
19 May 2015 Standards and Accreditation Bill 3403 
 
flexible, pragmatic, and proportional approach to managing actual and perceived 
conflicts of interest for standards development committee members.  
As I mentioned, the standards will continue to be developed using the committees of 
technical experts and the representatives of consumer and worker organisations. It is 
important that any conflicts of interest are identified and managed to ensure 
transparency and confidence in the standards development process. The bill now strikes 
a more appropriate balance between ensuring people with the right knowledge and 
expertise can participate in standards development committees and avoiding capture by 
a particular interest. The definition of “personally interested” has been altered to narrow 
the range of interests that it captures. Second, potential standards development 
committee members must disclose any interests to the Standards Executive before their 
membership is proposed to the Standards Approval Board, and on an ongoing basis if 
interests arise while they are on standards development committees. Third, the bill is 
now explicit that a chairman with statutory functions will be appointed for each 
standards development committee. The chairperson must not be personally interested.  
A new provision gives the chairperson a role in managing conflicts of interest in 
consultation with the Standards Executive. The Standards Executive will support the 
chairperson in man aging the conflict of interest. The register of interests relating to a 
standards development committee will be available to the Standards Approval Board 
when it is considering a draft standard for approval. This allows the board to have 
regard to the nature and extent of the interests when approving or declining a proposal.  
Another aspect I would like to highlight is the addition of provisions to clarify that 
New Zealand will continue to participate in standards development committees run by 
other standar ds organisations, such as Standards Australia. This has always been the 
intention, but the bill now makes it clear that the Standards Executive will propose New 
Zealand nominees for international and joint standards development committees, whom 
the board will approve or decline.  
Some changes were also made to clarify the existence of copyright in standards, 
which was a particular concern of some stakeholders. Other changes to the bill are 
minor and technical in nature and include the deletion of definitions no longer required.  
In conclusion, I once again thank the members of the Commerce Committee and 
those who provided submissions. I reiterate my view that the bill is stronger for having 
been through this process and is more able to provide a sustainable,  responsive
