RADIO NEW ZEALAND AMENDMENT BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister of Broadcasting) : I move, That the Radio New 
Zealand Amendment Bill be now read a second time . Most members of this House 
would agree that Radio New Zealand is an iconic insti tution in this country. Since it 
first broadcast on our airwaves in 1925, our public radio broadcaster has delighted and 
informed audiences of all generations. But even iconic institutions must adapt to the 
modern age or else they will grow irrelevant and eventually fade. That is why this 
Government is progressing this bill to futureproof our public broadcaster for years to 
come.  
The bill proposes two key changes. The first puts in place a new charter that reflects 
Radio New Zealand’s role as a modern publ ic broadcaster, and the second makes Radio 
New Zealand technology -neutral, so that it can reach audiences beyond its traditional 
base. Radio New Zealand receives Crown funding of more than $35 million a year, and 
in order to thrive and get best value for money in the decades to come, it must undergo a 
transformation from a traditional broadcaster to a multimedia organisation that connects 
with diverse audiences in a range of ways. The pressures of innovative technology and 
changing consumer demands are not new, nor are they unique to Radio New Zealand, 
19 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3427 
 
but these are the forces that are driving real and transformative change for our national 
radio service.  
Recent research by New Zealand On Air revealed some interesting findings about the 
way in which New Zea landers are using and accessing content. It confirmed that the 
traditional media forms of linear and live radio still attract the largest audiences in New 
Zealand, but online audiences are growing fast, especially amongst the younger 
demographics. The rese arch found that although New Zealanders are not necessarily 
abandoning one platform for another, we are consuming more content overall from a 
variety of sources. Digital platforms are playing a bigger part in our lives. Radio New 
Zealand has already been r esponsive to these changes and, although there has been a 
decline in listenership across traditional platforms, over the last 12 months its online 
audience has grown significantly as its multimedia strategy is implemented.  
The number of unique visitors to  the Radio New Zealand website is up 64 percent to 
600,000 a month. The youth -focused website The Wireless  is using the internet and 
digital media to reach different audiences. Around 30,000 unique users access this site a 
month—year-on-year growth of 71 p ercent. Requests for audio via platforms such as 
iTunes and apps have grown 90 percent in the last year. What this demonstrates is a 
strong demand for content online as well as the more traditional on air content. 
Although this shift to multiple platforms is encouraging, there is more work to be done, 
which is why this bill introduces a new and updated charter for Radio New Zealand.  
As outlined earlier, the bill incorporates a revision of the charter to better reflect 
Radio New Zealand’s role as a modern m ultimedia organisation. Under section 7(4) of 
the Radio New Zealand Act, Radio New Zealand’s charter must be reviewed by the 
House of Representatives at 5 -yearly intervals. The new charter is incorporated in what 
will be a new section 8 of the Act as subst ituted by clause 5 of the bill. Under the 
revised charter Radio New Zealand is expected to foster a sense of national identity by 
contributing to tolerance and understanding and by reflecting and promoting ethnic, 
cultural, and artistic diversity and expre ssion. It is to provide reliable, independent, and 
freely accessible news and information, a particularly important role in times of crises.  
The charter lays out expectations around programming. Radio New Zealand content 
is to inform and entertain the people of New Zealand, is to be challenging, innovative, 
and engaging, and is to foster critical thought and inform wide -ranging debate. The 
content is to be predominantly and distinctively of New Zealand, and to reflect New 
Zealand’s cultural identity, including Māori language and culture. At the same time 
Radio New Zealand’s programming is expected to provide an awareness of the world 
and New Zealand’s place in it.  
The new charter also affirms Radio New Zealand’s international statutory obligation 
to provide an international service in both English and Pacific languages to radio 
stations in the South Pacific. The charter identifies the diverse fo rms of cultural 
expression Radio New Zealand should support, including drama, comedy, literature, 
and the performing arts. Its support of New Zealand music, both in composition and 
performance, will continue. Radio New Zealand is expected to provide programmes that 
balance special interest with those of wide appeal, recognising the interests of all age 
groups.  
Finally, having created this tremendously broad range of radio material, Radio New 
Zealand is charged under the charter with preserving and archivin g broadcasting 
material of historical interest. In 2012 its holdings were transferred to the care of the 
New Zealand Film Archive, now known as Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision, as part of the 
Government’s objective of rationalising the care of, and access to, Ne w Zealand’s 
audiovisual heritage.  
3428 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 19 May 2015 
 
The new charter contains a new obligation to take advantage of the most effective 
means of delivery, including its website. The provision will help make Radio New 
Zealand technology-neutral so that it can reach audiences beyond the traditional listener 
at home to those using smartphones and other devices anywhere and anytime.  
As an early adopter of new media, Radio New Zealand is now well established as a 
multi-platform broadcaster, providing flexible listening options fo r its audiences. For 
example, in the financial year 2013 -14, 3.5 million podcasts were downloaded. Regular 
users of the Radio New Zealand mobile app grew by almost 62 percent during this time. 
Radio New Zealand’s website also offers live streaming, a text -based news service, and 
audio on demand. So although Radio New Zealand has made good progress, updating 
this legislation is important to enable Radio New Zealand to maximise the public value 
of content and help it to grow as a multi-platform broadcaster.  
I do want to signal that I have been asked by Radio New Zealand to undertake 
clarification at the Committee of the whole House stage to make clear that although 
Radio New Zealand services must remain commercial-free, this does not prevent it from 
taking ad vantage of opportunities such as, for example, its recent presence on 
iHeartRadio, which is, of course, in itself a commercial app that includes advertising, or 
licensing its content for re -use by commercial providers. At the same time changes will 
also need to be made to the commencement date of the legislation. We will also look to 
make the research obligations on Radio New Zealand more flexible without reducing its 
accountability.  
In concluding, the new charter affirms the breadth of programmes and serv ices New 
Zealanders expect from their public radio —services that could not be delivered by a 
broadcasting business that is wholly reliant on commercial revenue. New Zealanders 
greatly value Radio New Zealand as one of our most respected and indispensable 
cultural institutions, and this bill will futureproof it for generations to come. I look 
forward to further progressing it through the House.

override what they knew was going to be a drumming when they came into this House

legislation was, and they were made by the Minister about how terrible it was that it had

fascinatingly, eve n though it has changed almost not a jot since 2009, is now 
apparently—according to the speakers from the Government benches —going to 
completely update and modernise Radio New Zealand for the new digital age and for 
the many media platforms that are available now.

everything on the Order Paper and then eventually it will morph itself into the future.
